Part 1

Go Foundations

#1.1 History, philosophy, and design goals

Go was created at Google in 2007 by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson, and open-sourced in 2009. The motivating problem was concrete: Google's C++ and Java codebases had grown to the point where builds took many minutes, dependency graphs were tangled, and concurrency was painful enough that engineers avoided it.

The design goals, in the language authors' own framing:

  1. Fast compilation. The dependency model forbids unused imports and circular imports specifically so the compiler never has to do transitive header parsing. This is why Go refuses to compile a file with an unused import — an ergonomic cost paid deliberately for build speed.
  2. Simplicity over expressiveness. No inheritance, no method overloading, no exceptions, no operator overloading. The bet is that a language a team can hold entirely in their heads produces more maintainable systems than one with more powerful abstractions.
  3. Concurrency as a first-class primitive. Goroutines and channels are built into the language, not a library.
  4. A real standard library. HTTP servers, JSON, crypto, and compression ship with the language.
  5. Static binaries. go build produces a single executable with no runtime dependency, which is why Go dominates container-based deployment.

Comparison to other languages

ConcernGoJavaPythonRustNode.js
TypingStatic, inferredStatic, verboseDynamicStatic, inferredDynamic
MemoryGCGCGC (refcount)Ownership, no GCGC
ConcurrencyGoroutines (M:N)Threads + virtual threadsGIL, asyncioasync/await, threadsEvent loop
Startup~1ms~100ms+ (JVM)~50ms~1ms~30ms
BinarySingle staticJAR + JVMInterpreter + depsSingle staticRuntime + node_modules
Compile speedVery fastModerateN/ASlowN/A
Error handlingExplicit returnsExceptionsExceptionsResult<T,E>Exceptions/callbacks

The honest tradeoff: Go is deliberately less expressive than Rust or Scala. You will write more boilerplate. if err != nil will appear thousands of times in a large codebase. What you get is that a new engineer can be productive in your codebase in days rather than months, and that compile-test cycles are measured in seconds.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: Go's niche is network services — API servers, proxies, CLI tools, infrastructure daemons. Kubernetes, Docker, Terraform, Prometheus, etcd, and CockroachDB are all Go. It is a poor fit for CPU-bound numerical work (no SIMD ergonomics, GC pauses), GUI applications, and anything needing hard real-time guarantees.

Common pitfalls: Engineers arriving from Java or Python often try to recreate inheritance hierarchies or generic frameworks. Go resists this. The idiomatic path is small interfaces, concrete types, and composition — fighting that produces code that is awkward in both languages.

#1.2 Toolchain: go install, GOPATH vs Modules, go.mod/go.sum, workspaces

The historical GOPATH model (know it, don't use it)

Before Go 1.11, all code lived under a single $GOPATH/src directory tree, and import paths were filesystem paths relative to it. There was no versioning — go get fetched the tip of the default branch. This is why older tutorials tell you to put your project in ~/go/src/github.com/you/project. You should not do this. It's obsolete.

Modules (the current model)

A module is a collection of packages versioned as a unit, rooted at a directory containing go.mod.

That produces:

The module path (github.com/yourname/myservice) is both the identity of the module and the prefix for importing its packages. It does not have to be a real URL, but if you ever want others to go get it, it must match the repository location.

Adding a dependency:

go.mod after:

Direct vs indirect: direct dependencies are ones you import. Indirect are dependencies of your dependencies. The // indirect comment is maintained automatically.

go.sum

go.sum contains cryptographic hashes of every module version in your dependency graph, including ones you don't currently use but have used. It is a lock file for integrity, not for version selection — version selection lives in go.mod.

Two hashes per module: one for the module zip, one for its go.mod. If a published version is ever mutated, the hash mismatch fails your build loudly. Always commit go.sum.

Essential commands

go mod tidy is the one you'll run constantly. It is the canonical way to keep go.mod honest.

go install vs go get vs go build

This changed in Go 1.16+ and trips people up constantly:

  • go build — compiles the current module, writes a binary to the current directory.
  • go run — compiles and immediately runs, leaving no binary.
  • go install — compiles and installs a binary to $GOBIN (default ~/go/bin). Since 1.16, go install pkg@version installs a tool without modifying your go.mod. This is how you install CLI tools:
  • go get — since 1.17, this only manages dependencies in go.mod. It no longer installs binaries. If a tutorial tells you go get a CLI tool, it's pre-1.16.

Workspaces (go.work, Go 1.18+)

Workspaces solve local multi-module development. Suppose you have a service and a shared library, in separate repos, and you're changing both:

go.work:

Now service resolves sharedlib imports to your local checkout, ignoring the published version — without a replace directive polluting go.mod.

Do not commit go.work to a shared repository. It's a local development convenience; committing it changes the build for everyone. Add it to .gitignore.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: Monorepos with multiple services sharing internal libraries. Workspaces replaced the old workflow of replace directives that engineers constantly forgot to remove before merging.

Common pitfalls:

  • Committing go.work and breaking CI, which doesn't have the sibling directories.
  • Forgetting go mod tidy before commit, leaving stale requirements.
  • Using go get -u casually — it upgrades everything transitively and is a common source of surprise breakage. Prefer upgrading specific modules.

#1.3 Project layout conventions

There is no official Go project layout. There is a widely-cited community repository (golang-standards/project-layout) that is not endorsed by the Go team, and Russ Cox has publicly said it isn't a standard. Treat it as one opinion.

What is real and enforced by the compiler:

internal/ — the only compiler-enforced convention

Any package under a directory named internal/ can only be imported by code rooted at internal/'s parent.

If another module tries import "github.com/you/service/internal/auth", compilation fails. This is genuinely useful — it lets you refactor freely without worrying about downstream breakage.

A layout that works for backend services

The key ideas:

  • cmd/<name>/main.go for each binary. main.go should be thin — parse config, wire dependencies, start the server.
  • internal/ for everything that isn't a public API.
  • Layered dependencies flow inward. handler imports service, service imports repository, and domain imports nothing. Never the reverse.

The pkg/ debate

pkg/ is contentious. Arguments against: it adds a meaningless directory level, since Go already has import paths. Arguments for: it clearly signals "this is intended for external consumption" alongside internal/.

Recommendation: if your module is a service that nobody imports, skip pkg/ entirely and put everything in internal/. If you publish a library, put the public API at the module root.

Common pitfalls: Over-structuring a small service. A 500-line service does not need seven directories. Start flat, split when a file exceeds a few hundred lines or a clear boundary emerges.

#1.4 Basic syntax: variables, constants, iota, zero values, type inference

Variable declaration

:= is only legal inside a function body. At package level you must use var.

Zero values

Every type has a zero value, and variables are always initialized. There is no undefined behaviour from reading an uninitialized variable.

TypeZero value
int, int8…uint640
float32, float640.0
boolfalse
string"" (empty, not nil)
pointer, slice, map, channel, func, interfacenil
structstruct with all fields at their zero values
arrayarray with all elements at their zero values

This is a genuine design feature. It means var buf bytes.Buffer is immediately usable — the zero value of bytes.Buffer is an empty buffer ready to write to. Well-designed Go types make their zero value useful. sync.Mutex is another example: the zero value is an unlocked mutex.

Constants

Constants are compile-time values. They can be typed or untyped.

Untyped constants are one of Go's quieter good ideas. const Pi = 3.14159 can be assigned to a float32 or float64 without conversion, because it has no type until it's used.

iota

iota is a compile-time counter that resets to 0 at each const block and increments per ConstSpec line.

Common pitfalls with iota:

  • Reordering constants silently changes their numeric values. If those values are persisted to a database or sent over the wire, you've corrupted data. Never reorder an iota block whose values are serialized. Add new values at the end only.
  • The zero value is the first constant, so if StatusPending = 0, an unset Status field looks like "pending". Sometimes that's what you want; often you should burn 0 with _ so the zero value is invalid and bugs surface.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: enum-like status fields, permission bitmasks, HTTP retry strategies, log levels.

#1.5 Primitive types, type conversion vs type assertion, numeric precision

The type set

Use int unless you have a specific reason not to. Use sized types when you're matching a wire protocol, a database column, or minimizing struct size in a large array.

Conversion is always explicit

Go does no implicit numeric conversion. This is verbose and it is deliberate — it eliminates an entire class of bugs.

Conversion vs assertion — different operations

Type conversion changes a value's type at compile time: float64(i).

Type assertion extracts a concrete type from an interface at runtime: v.(string).

Numeric precision gotchas

Integer division truncates:

Overflow wraps silently. There is no panic.

This is a real production hazard. If you're computing a sum of user-supplied values, you must check for overflow yourself.

Floating point is not exact:

Never use floats for money. Use integer cents (int64), or a decimal library like shopspring/decimal. A rounding error of a fraction of a paisa, multiplied across millions of transactions, is a real accounting problem and a real audit finding.

Strings, bytes, and runes — the crucial distinction

A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes, conventionally UTF-8 encoded. It is not a sequence of characters.

Common pitfalls:

  • len(s) on a string with non-ASCII content is not the character count. Reversing a string by index corrupts multi-byte characters.
  • []byte(s) and string(b) both copy. In a hot loop this allocates. If you're only reading, use unsafe conversions carefully or restructure to avoid the conversion.
  • string(65) produces "A" (the rune), not "65". Use strconv.Itoa(65) for "65". Modern Go vets warn about this.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: validating user input lengths (a 20-character limit is not 20 bytes for Indian-language names), truncating text for display, database column sizing, generating URL slugs.

#1.6 Control flow

if

The initializer form keeps error variables scoped tightly, which matters when you have several in a function.

There are no parentheses around conditions, and braces are mandatory even for one-line bodies.

for — the only loop keyword

The loop variable capture change (Go 1.22) — critical

Before Go 1.22, i and v in a range loop were a single variable reused across iterations. This produced one of the most common Go bugs:

Under Go 1.21 and earlier, this typically prints 3 3 3 — all goroutines see the same variable after the loop finished. The fix was v := v inside the loop, or passing v as an argument.

Under Go 1.22 and later, each iteration gets a fresh variable, and this prints 1 2 3 in some order. The semantics are governed by the go directive in your go.mod — a module declaring go 1.21 keeps the old behaviour even on a newer toolchain.

This is version-sensitive and matters enormously. Verify your go.mod version line before relying on either behaviour. In code that must work on both, keep the explicit v := v.

switch

Type switch

In switch x := v.(type), x has the specific case's type inside each branch. Order matters when cases overlap — error before fmt.Stringer if a type satisfies both.

Labeled break and continue

Labels are also required to break out of a for from inside a select or switch, since a bare break there breaks the select/switch, not the loop. This is a genuine source of bugs in worker loops:

goto

Legal, rarely used. It cannot jump over variable declarations or into a block. Its main legitimate use is error cleanup in low-level code, and even there defer is usually better. If you're reaching for goto in application code, restructure instead.

Part 1 continues below.

#1.7 Functions: multiple returns, closures, method values

Multiple return values

Go functions return any number of values. The near-universal convention is (result, error).

Named returns are useful for documentation and for modifying the result in a deferred function. They are dangerous when overused — a naked return (return with no values) in a long function makes it hard to see what's actually returned. Use named returns for documentation, but still return values explicitly.

The one place naked returns earn their keep is deferred error modification:

This pattern matters. Ignoring Close() on a written file can silently lose data — the write may only be flushed at close time.

Variadic functions

A subtle trap: inside the function, nums is a slice that may alias the caller's backing array when you use nums.... Modifying it modifies the caller's slice.

Closures

A closure captures variables from its enclosing scope by reference.

The capture is by reference, not by value. This is the mechanism behind the loop-variable bug in §1.6, and behind memory leaks where a closure holding a large struct outlives the point you expected it to.

First-class functions and function types

The functional options pattern

This is the standard Go idiom for constructors with many optional parameters, and you will see it in nearly every serious library.

Why this beats a config struct: adding a new option is backward compatible, defaults live in one place, and invalid combinations can be rejected inside the option function.

Method values vs method expressions

Method values are what let you pass wg.Done directly to defer or a handler method to http.HandleFunc.

Common pitfall: a method value on a value receiver copies the receiver at the point the method value is created:

#1.8 Arrays vs slices — internals and pitfalls

This is the single most important section in Part 1. More Go bugs come from slice aliasing than from any other language feature.

Arrays are values

Arrays are rare in application code. They appear in fixed-size buffers, cryptographic digests ([32]byte from SHA-256), and as the backing store for slices.

Slice internals

A slice is a three-word header:

A slice is a view into an array. Copying a slice copies the header — three words — not the data. Two slices can share one backing array, which is where the trouble starts.

The append trap

append returns a new slice header. It may or may not allocate a new backing array. This conditional behaviour is the bug factory.

The same operation aliases or doesn't depending on capacity. You cannot reason about it locally.

The classic production bug

Fixes:

Rule of thumb: if you return a sub-slice of data you don't own, either use the three-index form or copy. If you accept a slice and store it in a struct, copy it — the caller may mutate it later.

Growth algorithm

When append exceeds capacity, the runtime allocates a larger array and copies. The growth factor is an implementation detail that has changed between releases — historically 2x for small slices, tapering toward 1.25x for large ones, with the threshold changing in Go 1.18. Do not depend on specific growth numbers; verify with your toolchain if it matters.

What you should depend on: preallocate when you know the size.

In a hot path this is often the single highest-impact optimization available. When you're building a result slice from a query returning n rows, make([]T, 0, n) matters.

nil slice vs empty slice

This matters for APIs. A nil slice marshals to null; an empty slice marshals to []. Frontend code that does data.items.length breaks on null. Always initialize slices you're returning in a JSON response:

Common slice operations

The memory leak pattern: deleting elements from a slice of pointers leaves the pointers in the backing array, keeping the pointed-to objects alive.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: request batching, pagination, buffer reuse in sync.Pool, parsing.

Part 1 review so far: if you cannot explain why append sometimes mutates a caller's data, re-read §1.8 before continuing.

#1.9 Maps — internals, iteration, concurrency rules

Basics

Reading a nil map is safe; writing panics. This bites when a struct has a map field that was never initialized.

The comma-ok idiom

Iteration order is deliberately randomized

This is intentional. The runtime starts iteration at a random bucket precisely so you cannot accidentally depend on order. If you need deterministic order, sort the keys:

Where this bites: tests that pass locally and fail in CI, JSON output that differs run to run breaking a diff-based test, and computing a hash over map contents.

Modifying during iteration

The spec says: entries added during iteration may or may not be produced. Entries deleted during iteration will not be produced. Deleting is defined behaviour and safe; adding is unpredictable.

Maps are NOT concurrency-safe

Note this is a fatal error, not a recoverable panic. The runtime has lightweight race detection built into the map implementation specifically because this bug was so common. You cannot recover() from it.

Safe alternatives:

Key type requirements

Map keys must be comparable with ==. Slices, maps, and functions are not comparable and cannot be keys.

Careful: a struct containing a slice field is not comparable, so it can't be a key. And a struct containing a float64 can be a key, but NaN != NaN, so a NaN key becomes permanently unreachable.

Maps of structs — the addressability rule

Map values are not addressable because the runtime may move entries during growth. Storing pointers is usually the cleaner choice for mutable values.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: in-memory caches, request deduplication, grouping query results, session stores, config lookup tables.

#1.10 Structs: embedding, tags, memory layout

Basics and embedding

Embedding is composition, not inheritance. There is no polymorphism here — Employee does not satisfy anything Person satisfies by virtue of being a "subclass," it satisfies it because the promoted method set genuinely includes Greet().

Embedding interfaces — a useful trick

This is how sort.Reverse works in the standard library. Embedding the interface gives you all its methods for free; you override only the one you care about.

Ambiguity in embedding

Ambiguity is only an error if you actually reference the ambiguous name. Depth wins: a field at depth 1 shadows one at depth 2.

Struct tags

Tags are string metadata read at runtime via reflection. The compiler does not validate them.

Tag conventions you'll meet: json, db/gorm, validate, yaml, bson (MongoDB), form, binding (Gin).

Critical pitfall: a typo in a tag is silently ignored. json:"nmae" compiles fine and produces the wrong output. go vet catches malformed tag syntax but not misspelled field names.

omitempty semantics

omitempty omits the field when it's the zero value: 0, "", false, nil, or an empty slice/map. It does not omit an empty struct.

This is a real problem: you cannot distinguish "field was zero" from "field was absent."

Use pointer fields for PATCH endpoints. It's the standard way to express tri-state (absent / null / value) in Go.

Comparing structs

For deep comparison of structs with slices/maps, use reflect.DeepEqual (slow, reflection-based) or google/go-cmp (better error messages, testing-oriented).

Memory layout, alignment, and padding

Struct fields are laid out in declaration order with padding inserted for alignment. Field order affects size.

Rule: order fields from largest to smallest alignment requirement.

Does this matter? Usually not. It matters when you have millions of instances — a cache with 10 million entries saves 80MB with that reordering. For a struct you allocate a hundred times, optimizing layout is premature. Use fieldalignment (part of golangci-lint) to find cases worth fixing.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: API request/response DTOs, database models, config structs, domain entities.

#1.11 Pointers: value vs pointer receivers, escape analysis

Pointer basics

There is no pointer arithmetic in Go. You cannot do p++ to walk an array. This is a safety decision — it makes the GC's job tractable and eliminates buffer-overrun bugs. The unsafe package provides an escape hatch, at the cost of losing all guarantees.

Value vs pointer receivers — the decision

Use a pointer receiver when:

  1. The method modifies the receiver.
  2. The struct is large (copying is expensive).
  3. The struct contains a sync.Mutex or other non-copyable field.
  4. Consistency — if any method needs a pointer receiver, use pointers for all of them.

Use a value receiver when:

  1. The type is small and immutable (time.Time, small value types).
  2. The type is a map, slice, or channel (already reference-like).
  3. You want the method available on both the value and pointer.

The consistency rule is the important one. A type with mixed receivers is confusing and can produce surprising method-set behaviour:

The method set rule: the method set of T includes methods with receiver T. The method set of *T includes methods with receiver T or *T. So a pointer satisfies more interfaces than a value.

Calling methods directly is more forgiving because Go auto-takes the address of an addressable value — d.Speak() becomes (&d).Speak(). But interface satisfaction has no such leniency. This distinction confuses nearly everyone at first.

Never copy a struct containing a mutex

go vet catches this with its copylocks check. Always run go vet.

Escape analysis

Go decides at compile time whether a value lives on the stack or heap. Stack allocation is nearly free and needs no GC; heap allocation costs an allocation plus eventual collection.

Check with:

Common causes of escape: returning a pointer to a local, storing a pointer in a struct that escapes, passing to interface{} (including fmt.Println — that's why it shows up in escape output constantly), capturing in a closure that escapes, and slices whose size isn't known at compile time.

Do not obsess over this. Write clear code, profile, and optimize escapes only in a demonstrated hot path. Returning &Point{} from a constructor is perfectly normal Go.

#1.12 Interfaces

Interfaces are where Go's design philosophy is most visible, and where engineers from other languages most often go wrong.

Implicit satisfaction

This is the key design decision. Because satisfaction is implicit, the consumer defines the interface, not the producer. You can write an interface that a third-party type satisfies without that library knowing your interface exists.

Accept interfaces, return structs

Returning a concrete struct lets callers use the full type; returning an interface prematurely hides functionality and makes evolution harder.

Small interfaces

The standard library's most-used interfaces have one method:

Go proverb: "The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction."

A one-method interface is trivially implementable and mockable. A ten-method interface forces every implementation to provide ten methods, most of which will be stubs.

Anti-pattern seen constantly in enterprise Go:

If only one implementation exists, this interface has negative value — it adds indirection and makes navigation harder. Define narrow interfaces at the point of consumption:

interface{} and any

any is a type alias for interface{}, added in Go 1.18. They're identical; any is preferred in new code.

An empty interface holds any value, and gives you no compile-time safety. Reach for generics (§1.14) before any in new code.

The nil interface trap

This is the single most-asked Go interview question, and a real production bug source.

Why: an interface value is a pair (type, value). It is nil only when both are nil. (*MyError, nil) has a type, so err != nil is true.

Rules to avoid it:

  1. Never declare a function's return type as a concrete error pointer type.
  2. Return the literal nil, never a typed nil variable.
  3. Prefer errors.New/fmt.Errorf over custom error types unless you need typed handling.

Compile-time interface checks

Put this line near the type definition. It costs nothing at runtime and catches breakage immediately when someone renames a method.

Interface embedding

This is how io.ReadWriteCloser and friends are built.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: dependency injection for testing, swapping a real database for an in-memory fake, pluggable cache backends, HTTP middleware chains.

Common pitfalls: defining interfaces before you have two implementations, the nil interface trap, huge interfaces mirroring an entire struct's method set.

#1.13 Error handling: error, wrapping, panic, defer

The error interface

That's the entire contract. Errors are values, not control flow.

Creating errors

Wrapping with %w (Go 1.13+)

Wrapping preserves the original error while adding context.

%w wraps. %v formats. Using %v where you meant %w silently breaks every errors.Is check downstream, and nothing warns you.

errors.Is, errors.As, errors.Unwrap

Is for sentinels, As for types. errors.As requires a pointer to the target type — &ve where ve is *ValidationError.

Wrapping multiple errors (Go 1.20+):

Custom Is and Unwrap

Error handling strategy for a service

The principle: wrap at each layer with context, inspect only at the boundary. Handlers translate errors into responses; services and repositories add context and propagate.

Do not log and return. If every layer logs, one failure produces five log lines. Log where you handle, return everywhere else.

defer

Arguments are evaluated at defer time, not at execution time:

Defer in a loop is a leak:

panic and recover

recover() only works inside a deferred function, and only in the goroutine that panicked.

When panic is appropriate:

  • Genuinely unrecoverable programmer errors during initialization (regexp.MustCompile, template.Must).
  • Impossible states that indicate a bug (default: in a switch over an exhaustive enum).

When it is not:

  • Anything the caller could reasonably handle. Return an error.
  • Across package boundaries. A library that panics on bad input is badly designed.

A panic in any goroutine crashes the whole process unless recovered in that goroutine:

This is why every worker goroutine in a production service needs a recovery wrapper — see §12.4.

Common pitfalls:

  • %v instead of %w, silently breaking the error chain.
  • Ignoring errors with _. errcheck in golangci-lint catches this.
  • Logging and returning the same error at every layer.
  • defer inside a loop.
  • Assuming recover() in main catches a panic in a goroutine. It does not.

#1.14 Generics (Go 1.18+)

Type parameters

Constraints

Without ~, Celsius would not satisfy Number — the constraint would only match float64 exactly.

Generic types

Note var zero T — the idiomatic way to produce a zero value of an unknown type parameter.

Type inference and its limits

Inference works from arguments. Return types alone cannot drive inference.

When generics help and when they hurt

Good uses:

  • Container types (cache, stack, set, queue).
  • Slice/map utility functions.
  • Reducing genuine duplication across identical code differing only in type.

Bad uses:

  • Where an interface would be clearer. If you need behaviour, use an interface. Generics are for when the type itself varies but the code is identical.
  • Premature generalization with one call site.
  • Deeply nested type parameters that make signatures unreadable.

Go proverb, still true post-generics: "A little copying is better than a little dependency." Two 8-line functions are often better than one clever generic one.

Note on performance: Go implements generics via GC-shape stenciling, which means implementations may be shared across types with the same memory layout. This can mean an indirection cost compared to hand-written monomorphic code. Do not assume generics are free — benchmark if it's in a hot path.

Standard library generics — slices and maps packages (Go 1.21+):

The maps.Keys iterator form is Go 1.23+. On 1.21–1.22 it was in golang.org/x/exp/maps with a different signature. Verify against your version.

#1.15 Packages and visibility

Exported vs unexported

Capitalization is the entire access-control mechanism.

There is no private, protected, or friend. Package is the unit of encapsulation, not the type. Two types in the same package can see each other's unexported fields.

init()

Order: imported packages fully initialize first, then package-level variables in dependency order, then init() functions, then main().

Use init() sparingly. It runs implicitly, cannot return an error, and makes testing harder because you cannot control when it happens. Prefer explicit initialization in main(). Its legitimate uses are registering a database driver (sql.Register) and registering an image format decoder.

Blank imports

This is how SQL drivers register themselves. It's a deliberate exception to "no unused imports."

Breaking import cycles

Go forbids circular imports entirely. If a imports b, b cannot import a.

Three fixes:

  1. Extract shared types into a third package.
  1. Define an interface at the consumer.
  1. Merge the packages. If two packages are genuinely mutually dependent, they may be one concept split for no reason.

Option 2 is usually the right answer in layered service code, and it falls out naturally from "accept interfaces."

#1.16 Modules deep dive

Semantic versioning and the major-version rule

Go enforces semver. v1.2.3 = major.minor.patch.

The import compatibility rule: if an import path is unchanged, the package must be backward compatible. This forces major versions ≥ 2 into the path:

Your go.mod for a v2 module must declare module github.com/user/lib/v2. This is jarring, but it means v1 and v2 of the same library can coexist in one build — which genuinely solves diamond dependency problems that break other ecosystems.

v0 has no compatibility guarantee. v0.x.y may break at any minor version.

Minimal Version Selection

Go does not resolve to the newest compatible version. It selects the minimum version that satisfies all requirements.

The consequence is that builds are reproducible without a lock file for version selection. Adding a dependency does not silently upgrade everything else. This is a genuinely better design than most package managers, and it's why Go builds rarely break spontaneously.

replace and exclude

replace only applies to the main module. If a library you depend on has a replace directive, it's ignored. This means replace is not a way to ship a patch to your users — they must add it themselves.

Prefer go.work over replace for local development, since it can't accidentally be committed into your published module.

Private modules

Without GOPRIVATE, Go tries to fetch your private module through proxy.golang.org, which fails with a confusing 404 or 410. This is one of the most common setup problems in company Go environments.

Proxy and checksum database

The proxy means a deleted GitHub repo doesn't break your build — the proxy retains an immutable copy. This solved Go's equivalent of the left-pad problem structurally.

Vendoring

Vendoring is largely unnecessary now that the proxy exists. It's still used where builds must work with no network at all, or where auditors require every dependency in the repo. Cost: a large repo and noisy diffs.

Upgrading safely

go get -u ./... on a large project will upgrade dozens of transitive dependencies at once. When something breaks, you won't know which one. Upgrade deliberately, in small batches.

Vulnerability scanning

govulncheck is better than generic dependency scanners because it does reachability analysis — it only reports vulnerabilities in code your program actually calls. Run it in CI.

#Part 1 Review Checklist

Part 2

Memory, Runtime, and Internals

This Part is what separates engineers who write Go from engineers who can diagnose why a Go service is slow at 3am.

#2.1 Stack vs heap, escape analysis, goroutine stacks

Two places values live

Stack: each goroutine has one. Allocation is a pointer bump; deallocation is automatic on return. Essentially free, no GC involvement.

Heap: shared across goroutines. Allocation costs real work; deallocation requires the garbage collector to prove nothing references the object.

Unlike C, you do not choose. The compiler decides via escape analysis. new(T) does not necessarily heap-allocate, and a plain struct literal is not necessarily on the stack.

Escape analysis rules

A value escapes to the heap when the compiler cannot prove it doesn't outlive its stack frame.

Inspect the compiler's decisions:

Common escape causes:

  1. Returning a pointer to a local.
  2. Storing a pointer into a heap-allocated structure.
  3. Passing to interface{} / any — this includes every fmt call.
  4. Capturing in a closure that escapes.
  5. Slices/maps whose size isn't a small compile-time constant.
  6. Sending on a channel.

Goroutine stacks grow

A goroutine starts with a small stack (historically 2KB — implementation detail, don't hard-code it). When it needs more, the runtime allocates a bigger stack, copies the contents, and adjusts pointers. This is why goroutines are cheap enough to have a million of them, whereas OS threads at 1-8MB each would exhaust memory at a few thousand.

The copying has a consequence: a stack-allocated value's address changes when the stack grows. This is fine because Go has no pointer arithmetic and the runtime fixes up all pointers, but it's why unsafe.Pointer arithmetic across a potential stack growth is undefined.

Practical guidance

Do not restructure code to avoid escapes speculatively. Returning &User{} from a constructor is normal and correct Go. The time to look at escape analysis is when you have a profile showing allocation pressure in a specific function, typically in a request hot path or a tight loop.

The genuinely high-value optimizations, in order:

  1. Preallocate slices with known capacity (make([]T, 0, n)).
  2. Reuse buffers with sync.Pool in high-throughput paths.
  3. Avoid interface{} boxing in hot loops.
  4. Pass small structs by value rather than pointer (avoids the escape entirely).

#2.2 The garbage collector

What it is

Go uses a concurrent, tri-color, mark-and-sweep, non-generational, non-compacting collector.

  • Concurrent: it runs alongside your program. It does not stop the world for the whole cycle.
  • Tri-color mark and sweep: objects are conceptually white (unreached), grey (reached, children not yet scanned), black (reached and fully scanned). The GC starts from roots (globals, goroutine stacks), greys them, then processes greys to black until none remain. Whatever is still white is garbage.
  • Non-generational: unlike the JVM, Go does not segregate young and old objects. The Go team's position is that escape analysis already keeps most short-lived data on the stack, so a nursery buys less than it costs.
  • Non-compacting: objects don't move. Addresses are stable. This is why Go can safely pass pointers to cgo.

Stop-the-world pauses

There are two brief STW phases per cycle (mark setup and mark termination). Modern Go targets sub-millisecond pauses, typically well under 500µs even with large heaps. Pause time is largely decoupled from heap size, which is the key achievement of the design.

However: low pause time is bought with CPU. The GC uses roughly 25% of available CPU during a cycle by default, and assist mechanics can slow down allocating goroutines directly. If your service is allocation-heavy, GC shows up as throughput loss and latency variance, not as long pauses.

Tuning: GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT

GOGC (default 100) sets the heap growth target. At GOGC=100, a new cycle starts when the heap reaches 2× the live heap size after the last collection.

GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19+) sets a soft memory ceiling. The GC becomes more aggressive as you approach it.

This is the single most valuable GC knob for containerized services. The classic failure mode: a container has a 2GB limit, the Go heap grows past it, and the kernel OOM-kills the process with no Go-level error, no stack trace, and no useful log line. GOMEMLIMIT lets the GC push back before that happens.

Recommended production setting:

For a service with a large stable cache, a common pattern is GOGC=off plus GOMEMLIMIT — the GC then runs only when approaching the limit, rather than repeatedly scanning a heap that is mostly long-lived.

Setting them from code:

Reducing GC pressure

The GC's cost scales with the number of pointers it must scan, not bytes allocated. A []int of a million elements is one scan-free object; a []*int of a million elements is a million pointers to chase.

Techniques that actually work:

  1. Prefer []T over []*T for collections of small structs.
  2. Preallocate. Reallocation churns the heap.
  3. sync.Pool for objects reused across requests (buffers, encoders).
  4. Avoid interface{} in hot paths — boxing allocates.
  5. Reuse byte buffers rather than allocating per request.

sync.Pool caveats: the pool is cleared at every GC cycle, so it is a cache for allocation churn, not a persistent object pool. Forgetting Reset() is a data-leak bug — you can serve one user's buffer contents to another. And don't pool objects whose sizes vary wildly; you'll retain the largest ones forever.

Observing GC

Reading it: 4->4->1 MB is heap-at-start → heap-at-end → live-heap. 5 MB goal is the next trigger. The three clock numbers are STW-mark-setup + concurrent-mark + STW-mark-termination.

In code:

ReadMemStats stops the world. Do not call it per-request. Expose it as a metric on a timer instead.

Where this shows up in real backend systems: a service whose p99 latency degrades under load with no obvious slow query is very often GC assist pressure. GOMEMLIMIT misconfiguration in Kubernetes is one of the most common causes of unexplained OOMKills.

#2.3 The scheduler: the GMP model

The three entities

  • G (Goroutine): a function with its own stack and state. Cheap — a few KB.
  • M (Machine): an OS thread. Actually executes code.
  • P (Processor): a scheduling context holding a local run queue of Gs. The number of Ps is GOMAXPROCS, defaulting to the number of CPU cores.

An M must hold a P to run Go code. The scheduler multiplexes many Gs onto few Ms — an M:N model.

Work stealing

When a P's local queue empties, it:

  1. Checks the global run queue.
  2. Polls the network poller for ready goroutines.
  3. Steals half the goroutines from a random other P.

This keeps all cores busy without a central lock on every scheduling decision.

Blocking behaviour — the important part

Blocking syscall (file I/O, cgo call): the M blocks in the kernel. The scheduler detaches the P from that M and hands it to another M, so the other goroutines on that P keep running. Your program does not stall.

Network I/O: does not block an M. Go's netpoller (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) parks the goroutine and frees the M immediately. When the socket is ready, the goroutine is rescheduled. This is the core reason Go handles high-concurrency network services so well — you write blocking-looking code and get async I/O performance.

Channel operations and mutex contention: the goroutine is parked, M keeps running other goroutines.

A tight CPU loop with no function calls: historically could starve a P. Since Go 1.14, the runtime uses signal-based asynchronous preemption, so even for {} gets preempted. Pre-1.14, that loop could hang the whole program during a GC.

GOMAXPROCS and containers

The container problem, and it's a big one. In Kubernetes with resources.limits.cpu: "2", runtime.NumCPU() returns the host's core count — possibly 64 — because Go reads the CPU count, not the cgroup CFS quota. So Go creates 64 Ps on a container allowed 2 cores' worth of CPU time. The result is heavy context switching, CFS throttling, and latency spikes.

Fix: use go.uber.org/automaxprocs, which reads the cgroup quota:

Or set it explicitly in your deployment manifest. This is one of the highest-value single-line changes for containerized Go services and it is routinely missed.

(Note: newer Go versions have been improving container awareness. Check the release notes for your version — but automaxprocs remains the safe default.)

Cooperative vs preemptive

Go's scheduler is mostly cooperative with asynchronous preemption as a backstop. Goroutines yield at function calls (via stack-growth checks), channel operations, syscalls, and runtime.Gosched(). Since 1.14, signals preempt long-running loops.

You should essentially never need runtime.Gosched(). If you think you do, you probably have a design problem.

#2.4 Compilation, cross-compilation, build tags, cgo

How go build works

  1. Parse and type-check each package.
  2. Compile each package to an object file (parallelized across packages).
  3. Link into a single static binary.

The build cache (~/.cache/go-build) means unchanged packages aren't recompiled. go clean -cache clears it if you suspect corruption.

Useful build flags

Reading injected version info:

Cross-compilation

This is one of Go's genuinely great features. From a Mac you can build a Linux ARM binary with no toolchain setup:

Caveat: cross-compilation only works this smoothly with CGO_ENABLED=0. Any cgo dependency requires a cross-compiling C toolchain, which is where the simplicity ends.

Build tags

The //go:build line must appear before the package clause with a blank line after it. The older // +build syntax is deprecated but still seen in existing code.

Filename suffixes work implicitly: file_linux.go, file_windows.go, file_amd64.go, file_test.go.

A practical use — separating integration tests:

cgo and its real costs

What cgo costs you:

  1. Cross-compilation breaks. You now need a C cross-toolchain.
  2. Slow builds. The C compiler runs on every build.
  3. Call overhead. A cgo call is far more expensive than a Go call — it involves a stack switch and scheduler coordination. In a tight loop this dominates.
  4. The goroutine's M blocks for the duration of the C call, consuming a thread.
  5. No stack growth in C. cgo calls run on a separate, fixed system stack.
  6. Manual memory management. Go's GC does not see C allocations.
  7. CGO_ENABLED=0 no longer works, so you lose scratch/distroless containers and static linking.
  8. Debugging is much harder. Panics through the C boundary produce unhelpful traces.

Where you'll hit it anyway: SQLite (mattn/go-sqlite3), some crypto libraries, os/user and DNS resolution in the standard library under certain conditions.

Guidance: avoid cgo unless there is no pure-Go alternative. For SQLite, modernc.org/sqlite is a pure-Go translation that avoids all of the above. The Go proverb: "Cgo is not Go."

#2.5 Reflection and unsafe

reflect basics

Modifying through reflection

To modify, you need a pointer and must call .Elem():

Reflection's real cost

Reflection is roughly an order of magnitude slower than direct field access, and it defeats compiler optimizations and inlining. Rough guidance rather than precise benchmarks: assume reflective field access costs tens of nanoseconds versus sub-nanosecond direct access. Measure on your own hardware — the ratio varies with Go version and workload.

Where reflection is legitimately used:

  • encoding/json, encoding/xml, yaml
  • ORMs (GORM)
  • Validation libraries (go-playground/validator)
  • Dependency injection frameworks
  • fmt verbs like %v

Where you should not use it: application code. If you find yourself writing reflection in a handler or service, there is almost always a better design with interfaces or generics.

The Go proverb: "Clear is better than clever. Reflection is never clear."

unsafe

Rules if you must use unsafe:

  1. It voids the Go 1 compatibility promise. Your code may break on any Go release.
  2. It disables type safety entirely.
  3. go vet has an unsafeptr check — heed it.
  4. The unsafe.Pointer conversion rules in the package documentation are load-bearing. Violating them can produce GC crashes that appear months later in unrelated code.

Legitimate uses: Sizeof/Alignof/Offsetof for struct layout analysis; zero-copy string/byte conversion in a proven hot path; interop with C memory layouts.

Everything else: don't. The performance win is rarely worth the class of bug you're inviting.

#Part 2 Review Checklist

Part 3

Concurrency

Go's headline feature. Also where the hardest production bugs live.

The governing proverb: "Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating."

And its underrated companion: "Concurrency is not parallelism." Concurrency is structuring a program as independently executing pieces. Parallelism is executing pieces simultaneously. Go gives you concurrency primitives; whether they run in parallel depends on GOMAXPROCS and your hardware.

#3.1 Goroutines and goroutine leaks

Creation

Three rules visible here:

  1. wg.Add(1) goes before go, never inside the goroutine — otherwise Wait() can return before the goroutine starts.
  2. wg.Done() is always deferred.
  3. Pass loop variables as arguments (required pre-1.22, still good documentation post-1.22).

Goroutines are cheap but not free

A goroutine costs a few KB of stack plus scheduler bookkeeping. A million is feasible; a million doing real work with real buffers is not. Unbounded goroutine creation is a genuine production failure mode:

Use a bounded worker pool (§3.5) instead.

Goroutine leaks — the four causes

A leaked goroutine is one that never terminates. It holds its stack, everything its stack references, and any resources it opened, forever. Leaks are silent — memory climbs, and nothing errors.

Leak 1: blocked send with no receiver

Fix: buffer the channel so the send can complete, or use select with a done channel.

Leak 2: blocked receive with no sender

Fix: always close() channels when done producing, or add a cancellation path.

Leak 3: forgotten context cancellation

go vet's lostcancel check catches this. Run it.

Leak 4: infinite loop with no exit condition

The cancellable goroutine pattern

Every long-lived goroutine should have exactly one way to be told to stop:

Note the nested select on the result send. A worker that blocks sending a result when nobody is receiving is itself a leak.

Detecting leaks

In production, expose runtime.NumGoroutine() as a Prometheus gauge. A monotonically climbing goroutine count is the clearest possible leak signal.

In tests, use go.uber.org/goleak:

And in a live service, /debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2 dumps every goroutine's stack — the fastest way to see where they're stuck.

#3.2 Channels

Unbuffered vs buffered

Unbuffered channels are a synchronization primitive, not just a queue. The send and receive happen at the same instant — a rendezvous.

Choosing a buffer size: the honest answer is that buffer size is a backpressure decision. Size 0 means the producer runs at exactly the consumer's speed. A large buffer lets the producer race ahead, hiding a throughput mismatch until memory runs out. Prefer unbuffered or small buffers unless you have a specific reason — a buffer sized to the number of workers, for instance.

Channel state behaviour — the table to memorize

Operationnil channelopen, emptyopen, has dataopen, fullclosed
Sendblocks foreverblocks (unbuf) / succeeds (buf)succeedsblockspanic
Receiveblocks foreverblockssucceedssucceedsreturns zero value immediately
Closepanicsucceedssucceedssucceedspanic

The three panic cases — send on closed, close of closed, close of nil — are runtime panics that will crash your service.

The nil-channel blocking behaviour is useful, not just a hazard — see the select section.

Who closes a channel

The sender closes. Never the receiver. A receiver that closes can cause the sender to panic. This is the single most important channel convention.

If no producer can safely close (e.g. producers may be cancelled at arbitrary times), use a separate done channel for signalling rather than closing the data channel.

Directional channels

Use directional parameters. They document intent and let the compiler catch a receiver trying to close.

The done-channel idiom

Closing a channel broadcasts. Every goroutine receiving from it unblocks. This is why close(done) is the idiomatic cancellation signal rather than sending N values.

chan struct{} communicates "this channel carries no data, only signal," and struct{}{} occupies zero bytes.

#3.3 select

Basics

If multiple cases are ready, one is chosen uniformly at random. This prevents starvation but means you cannot express priority directly in a select.

Non-blocking with default

Timeouts

time.After leaks in a loop. Each call allocates a timer that lives until it fires. In a loop running thousands of iterations per second with a 30-second timeout, you accumulate a large number of live timers.

The Stop/drain/Reset dance is genuinely awkward. (Timer semantics were simplified in Go 1.23 — check the release notes for your version; on 1.23+ the drain step may be unnecessary.) In most real code, use context.WithTimeout instead, which handles this for you.

The nil-channel disable trick

Setting a channel variable to nil removes its case from select permanently, since receiving from nil blocks forever. This is the clean way to handle a merge where one input finishes first:

Without the nil trick, a closed channel returns immediately forever and spins the loop at 100% CPU. This is a real bug people ship.

Empty select

select {} blocks forever. Occasionally used to park main in a server that runs entirely in goroutines — but a signal handler is a better choice in production.

#3.4 The sync package

sync.Mutex

Mutex rules:

  • Not reentrant. Locking twice in the same goroutine deadlocks.
  • Zero value is unlocked — no initialization needed.
  • Never copy a locked mutex. Always use pointer receivers. go vet catches copies.
  • Always defer Unlock() unless you have a measured reason to unlock earlier.

sync.RWMutex

RWMutex helps when reads heavily outnumber writes. Under a balanced or write-heavy load it is slower than a plain Mutex because of the extra bookkeeping. Benchmark before assuming it's an upgrade.

Never upgrade a read lock to a write lock by calling Lock() while holding RLock(). That deadlocks. Release, reacquire, and re-check your invariant.

sync.WaitGroup

Writing to distinct indices of a slice from multiple goroutines is safe — no two goroutines touch the same memory. Appending to a shared slice from multiple goroutines is not safe.

sync.Once

once.Do guarantees the function runs exactly once and that all callers block until it completes. If the function panics, Once still considers it done — it will not retry. For initialization that can fail, capture the error:

Note this means a failed init is permanent. If you need retry, use a mutex and a boolean instead.

sync.Map — read the fine print

sync.Map is not a general-purpose concurrent map. It is optimized for two specific cases stated in its own documentation: (1) an entry is written once and read many times, and (2) multiple goroutines read, write, and overwrite disjoint key sets.

For anything else, a plain map guarded by a RWMutex is usually faster and always more readable — plus it's type-safe, whereas sync.Map uses any.

Default to map + RWMutex. Reach for sync.Map only with a benchmark showing it wins for your access pattern.

sync/atomic

The typed atomic types (Go 1.19+) are better than the older atomic.AddInt64(&x, 1) functions because they make it structurally impossible to accidentally access the variable non-atomically.

Atomics are for single values only. If you need two fields to change together consistently, you need a mutex. Atomics are meaningfully faster for simple counters — use them for metrics, flags, and sequence numbers.

sync.Cond

Rarely needed. Use it when goroutines must wait for a condition that a channel can't express well:

In practice a buffered channel does this job more clearly. sync.Cond earns its place for broadcast-to-many-waiters on a complex predicate.

#3.5 Concurrency patterns

Bounded worker pool

The most important pattern in backend Go.

Sizing the pool: for CPU-bound work, runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0). For I/O-bound work, higher — but bounded by what the downstream can take. A pool of 500 workers hitting a database with 20 connections just queues at the pool.

Semaphore via buffered channel

When you want bounded concurrency without a full worker pool:

golang.org/x/sync/semaphore provides a weighted version with context support if you need it.

Pipeline

Each stage runs concurrently. Note that this simple version has no cancellation — a real pipeline needs a ctx threaded through each stage, or the goroutines leak if the consumer stops early.

Fan-out / fan-in

Rate limiting

golang.org/x/time/rate is the right answer for in-process rate limiting. For distributed rate limiting across replicas, you need Redis — covered in Part 9.

Singleflight — deduplicating concurrent identical work

This is the standard defence against cache stampede: when a hot cache key expires and 1000 requests all miss simultaneously, singleflight ensures exactly one hits the database. More in Part 9.

#3.6 context

context is how cancellation, deadlines, and request-scoped values propagate through a call tree. Every function that does I/O in a request path should accept one.

The rules

  1. ctx is always the first parameter, conventionally named ctx.
  2. Never store a Context in a struct. Pass it explicitly. (Rare exceptions exist for struct types that are themselves request-scoped.)
  3. Never pass a nil Context. Use context.TODO() if you don't have one yet.
  4. Always call cancel, usually via defer.
  5. WithValue is for request-scoped data crossing API boundaries, not for optional parameters.

Constructors

The two sentinel errors are context.Canceled and context.DeadlineExceeded. Distinguish them — a deadline exceeded is often worth logging as slow; a cancellation usually means the client hung up and is not an error worth alerting on.

Propagation through a call chain

The whole point: when the HTTP client disconnects, r.Context() is cancelled, which cancels the DB query mid-flight and aborts the outbound HTTP call. Without context plumbing, your service keeps burning database CPU on a query nobody will read.

Always use the ...Context variants: QueryContext, ExecContext, QueryRowContext, BeginTx, http.NewRequestWithContext.

Checking cancellation in a loop

For expensive per-item work, check every iteration. For cheap work, check every N iterations — the select itself has a cost.

WithValue — use sparingly

Why the custom key type matters: if you use a plain string key, another package using the same string silently overwrites your value. An unexported named type makes collision impossible.

What belongs in WithValue: request ID, trace/span context, authenticated user identity, locale. Things that genuinely cross every layer.

What does not: function parameters. If a function needs a limit, take it as an argument. Context values are untyped, invisible in the signature, and a lookup failure is a runtime bug rather than a compile error.

Context in an HTTP server

#3.7 Race conditions and the race detector

What a data race is

A data race occurs when two goroutines access the same memory concurrently and at least one is a write, with no synchronization between them. The result is undefined — not merely a wrong value, but genuinely unspecified behaviour.

counter++ is three operations: load, add, store. Two goroutines can both load 5, both compute 6, both store 6 — one increment vanishes.

The race detector

Output:

Run every CI test suite with -race. This is non-negotiable for a concurrent service. The cost is 5-10× slowdown and 5-10× memory, so don't ship a race-enabled binary to production — but do run it in CI, and consider running it in staging.

Critical limitation: the race detector only reports races that actually occur during execution. It is not static analysis. A race on a code path your tests don't exercise will not be found. Good test coverage of concurrent paths is what makes it effective.

Common races beyond the obvious

Racing on a map:

Racing via a captured loop variable (pre-1.22 — see §1.6).

Racing on a slice append:

append may reallocate and reassign the slice header — three words written non-atomically. Two concurrent appends can lose data or corrupt the header.

Racing on struct fields that "look independent":

False sharing

Two variables on the same 64-byte CPU cache line cause cache invalidation traffic even when logically independent. This is a performance problem, not a correctness one, and the race detector won't flag it.

Only do this with a benchmark proving it helps. It's a real technique in high-throughput counters and lock-free structures, and premature everywhere else.

#3.8 Deadlocks and livelocks

Deadlock: everyone waits forever

Go's runtime detects the case where every goroutine is blocked and panics with a helpful message. It cannot detect a partial deadlock where some goroutines still run — that just looks like a hang.

Lock ordering deadlock

The classic:

The rule: establish a global lock ordering and never deviate. Sort by a stable identifier — an ID, a memory address, a name.

Other deadlock causes

Cause 4 is common in growing codebases. The fix is to split each method into a public locking wrapper and a private non-locking implementation:

Livelock

Goroutines are running but making no progress — each politely yielding to the other. Rarer than deadlock and harder to spot because CPU usage looks healthy.

Prevention: add randomized backoff to retry loops rather than fixed delays, so competing actors desynchronize.

Diagnosing a hang in production

Enabling the profiles:

A goroutine dump showing hundreds of goroutines stuck at the same line is the fastest possible diagnosis of a hang. Make sure pprof is available in production, bound to localhost, and reachable via a debug sidecar or kubectl port-forward.

#3.9 errgroup

golang.org/x/sync/errgroup combines WaitGroup with error propagation and context cancellation. It is the right tool for "run N things concurrently, fail fast if any fails."

Why this is the right pattern for a service: three independent backend calls that would take 190ms sequentially take 80ms concurrently, and if any one fails, the other two are cancelled immediately rather than continuing to burn resources.

Bounding concurrency with errgroup

SetLimit gives you a bounded pool with error handling in four lines. For most "process this batch concurrently" tasks, this replaces a hand-rolled worker pool entirely.

Two things to watch:

  • g.Wait() returns only the first error. If you need all of them, collect errors into a slice guarded by a mutex, or use errors.Join.
  • Each g.Go closure must not write to shared state without synchronization. Writing distinct struct fields (as above) is fine; appending to a shared slice is not.

#Part 3 Review Checklist

Part 4

Testing, Tooling, and Code Quality

#4.1 The testing package

Test files end in _test.go and live in the same package (white-box) or package foo_test (black-box, forces you to use only the public API).

t.Error/t.Errorf record a failure and continue. t.Fatal/t.Fatalf record and stop the test immediately. Use Fatal when continuing would panic (a nil result you're about to dereference); Error when you want to see all failures at once.

Table-driven tests — the Go standard

t.Run gives each case its own name in output and lets you run one: go test -run 'TestDivide/by_zero'. Spaces in names become underscores.

Parallel subtests

t.Parallel() pauses the subtest until the parent returns, then runs all parallel subtests together. Deferred cleanup in the parent runs before parallel subtests finish — use t.Cleanup instead of defer when mixing.

Test helpers

t.Helper() is the difference between a useful failure line and one pointing at your helper. t.Cleanup is preferable to defer because it composes with subtests and runs in LIFO order.

TestMain

One per package. Use it for expensive shared setup — a test database, a Docker container via testcontainers-go.

Useful flags

-count=1 is the idiomatic way to defeat caching — Go caches passing test results keyed on inputs, which surprises people debugging flaky tests.

Coverage is a diagnostic, not a target. 100% coverage of trivial getters tells you nothing; 60% covering every error branch in your payment path tells you a lot. Chasing the number produces tests that assert nothing.

#4.2 Benchmarking

Output:

B/op and allocs/op are usually more actionable than ns/op. Driving allocations to zero in a hot path is a concrete, verifiable win.

The compiler-optimization trap

A benchmark reporting 0.25 ns/op for anything non-trivial is a red flag that the work was optimized away.

Install benchstat: go install golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat@latest. Single benchmark runs are noisy; -count=10 plus benchstat tells you whether a difference is real.

#4.3 Mocking, interfaces, and dependency injection

Hand-written fakes — usually the best option

For narrow interfaces, a hand-written fake is clearer than any generated mock and has no dependencies.

gomock

Worth it for wide interfaces where hand-writing every method is tedious. Note go.uber.org/mock is the maintained fork; the original golang/mock is archived.

testify

require for preconditions, assert for the actual assertions. Testify is ubiquitous but not universal — the Go team prefers plain if got != want. Either is defensible; be consistent within a codebase.

Dependency injection

Manual DI is the Go default and it is fine:

Explicit, greppable, no magic. This scales further than people expect — a 50-service wiring function is still readable.

google/wire generates this wiring at compile time when it gets tedious:

wire generates real Go code you can read — unlike reflection-based containers (uber-go/dig, fx), which move errors from compile time to runtime. Prefer wire if you use anything.

#4.4 httptest

Testing an outbound HTTP client

httptest.NewServer starts a real server on a random port. This is far better than mocking http.Client — you exercise real serialization, real headers, real status handling.

httptest.NewTLSServer for HTTPS; use srv.Client() to get a client that trusts its certificate.

#4.5 Fuzzing (Go 1.18+)

Failing inputs are written to testdata/fuzz/<FuzzName>/ and become permanent regression tests, replayed on every subsequent go test.

What to fuzz: parsers, decoders, anything consuming untrusted input, anything with an inverse operation you can assert as a property. Fuzzing finds panics, infinite loops, and invariant violations that example-based tests miss.

#4.6 Static analysis

go vet — ships with Go, run it always

Catches: Printf format/argument mismatches, struct tags that are malformed, unreachable code, copied locks (copylocks), lost context cancel (lostcancel), shadowed errors, misuse of sync.WaitGroup.

go test runs a subset of vet automatically.

staticcheck and golangci-lint

A production .golangci.yml:

The highest-value linters for a backend service: errcheck, bodyclose, sqlclosecheck, rowserrcheck, contextcheck, errorlint, nilerr. Those six catch resource leaks and broken error chains — real production bugs, not style nits.

Run in CI as a required check. Fixing lint findings retroactively across a large codebase is painful; enforcing from day one costs nothing.

#4.7 Profiling with pprof

Enabling it

Bind to localhost only. pprof endpoints leak internals and allow an attacker to trigger expensive profiles as a DoS.

The five profiles

Reading a profile

go tool pprof -http=:8081 profile.pb.gz opens an interactive browser UI with a flame graph — the fastest way to read a profile. In a flame graph, width is time. Look for the widest boxes, not the tallest stacks.

Benchmark-driven profiling

Execution tracer

The tracer shows goroutine scheduling, GC events, syscall blocking, and network waits on a timeline. Use it when pprof says "not much CPU" but latency is bad — that means you're waiting, and the tracer shows what for.

#4.8 Code generation

go generate is not run by go build — it is an explicit, manual step whose output you commit.

stringer is the canonical example: it turns an iota enum into a real String() method, so you never hand-maintain that switch.

Commit generated code. It keeps builds reproducible, makes code review show the effect of a schema change, and means contributors don't need the generator installed.

#4.9 Debugging with Delve

goroutines and goroutine N are Delve's real superpower — no other debugger handles Go's concurrency model as well. When a service hangs, attaching and listing goroutines finds the culprit in seconds.

Headless mode for remote or IDE debugging:

Print-statement debugging is still legitimate. For concurrency bugs, well-placed logging often beats a debugger, because stopping at a breakpoint changes the timing you're trying to observe.

#Part 4 Review Checklist

Part 5

Standard Library Deep Dive

#5.1 net/http from scratch

You can build a complete production HTTP service with no framework. Understanding this makes framework choices informed rather than cargo-culted.

Handler and HandlerFunc

Routing (Go 1.22+ enhanced ServeMux)

Go 1.22 added method matching and path wildcards to the standard mux, which removes the main reason to reach for a router library.

Pre-1.22 you had to match methods manually inside the handler, which is why gorilla/mux and chi became standard. Verify your Go version before relying on this.

Middleware without a framework

A caveat on wrapping ResponseWriter: your wrapper loses any optional interfaces the original implemented (http.Flusher, http.Hijacker, io.ReaderFrom). If you need streaming or WebSocket upgrades through your middleware, implement those interfaces on the wrapper too.

Production server configuration

http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil) has no timeouts at all. A client that opens a connection and never sends anything holds a goroutine and a file descriptor indefinitely. Always construct an http.Server explicitly. This is the single most common production mistake in Go HTTP services.

http.Client configuration

Three things people get wrong:

  1. http.DefaultClient has no timeout. A hung upstream hangs your goroutine forever. Never use it in production.
  2. MaxIdleConnsPerHost defaults to 2. If you call one upstream heavily, you're opening and closing TCP connections constantly. Raising this is often a large latency win.
  3. Not draining the body. defer resp.Body.Close() is necessary but not sufficient for connection reuse — you must also read the body to EOF, or the connection cannot return to the pool:

Create one http.Client and reuse it. A new client per request creates a new connection pool per request, defeating keep-alives entirely.

#5.2 encoding/json

Custom marshalling

Note MarshalJSON on a value receiver and UnmarshalJSON on a pointer receiver — unmarshalling must modify.

The pitfalls

1. Numbers become float64 in map[string]interface{}:

This silently corrupts large IDs — a real problem with Twitter-style snowflake IDs and database bigints.

2. Unknown fields are ignored by default:

Useful for internal APIs where you want strictness; risky for public APIs where clients may send extra fields legitimately.

3. omitempty cannot distinguish absent from zero — see §1.10. Use pointers for PATCH.

4. Unexported fields are silently skipped. No error, no warning.

5. Cyclic references cause infinite recursion and a stack overflow, not a clean error.

6. time.Time marshals as RFC3339. If your API contract says otherwise, you need a custom type.

7. HTML escaping is on by default: < becomes \u003c. Disable with enc.SetEscapeHTML(false) if you're not embedding output in HTML.

Limiting request body size

Without this, a client can send a multi-gigabyte body and exhaust your memory. This is a required defence on every endpoint that decodes a body.

#5.3 io and bufio

Buffering

Two classic bugs: forgetting scanner.Err() (so a read error looks like clean EOF), and forgetting w.Flush() on a bufio.Writer (so the last buffer's worth of output vanishes).

#5.4 The time package

Monotonic vs wall clock

time.Now() returns a Time containing both a wall clock reading and a monotonic reading. Subtraction uses the monotonic clock, so time.Since is immune to NTP adjustments and DST. But t.Round(0) strips the monotonic part, and a Time that has been serialized and deserialized has no monotonic reading.

Never measure a duration by subtracting two wall-clock timestamps that crossed a serialization boundary.

Timers vs tickers

A Ticker that is never stopped leaks the ticker goroutine and its channel. Always defer ticker.Stop().

Common gotchas

  • time.Parse assumes UTC when the layout has no timezone. Use ParseInLocation.
  • Storing local times in a database without a zone loses information. Store UTC, convert at the presentation layer.
  • AddDate(0, 1, 0) on 31 January gives 3 March (normalization), not 28/29 February. Handle month-end explicitly if it matters for billing.
  • time.Time comparison with == compares the monotonic reading and location too. Use .Equal().
  • LoadLocation needs the tzdata files. In a scratch container they don't exist. Either use a distroless base that includes them, copy /usr/share/zoneinfo, or import _ "time/tzdata" to embed the database in your binary (adds ~450KB).

#5.5 os and path/filepath

Path traversal defence — critical when a path comes from user input:

Without this, ../../etc/passwd reads whatever it likes. filepath.Join alone does not protect you — it cleans the path but the result can still escape.

Use filepath not path. path is for URL paths and always uses /; filepath is OS-aware.

#5.6 log and log/slog

The standard log package is unstructured and has no levels. For production, use log/slog (Go 1.21+).

Request-scoped logging

Now every log line in a request automatically carries the request ID — the single most useful thing you can do for debugging distributed systems.

Rules:

  • Never log secrets. No passwords, tokens, API keys, full card numbers, or connection strings. Redact at the source.
  • Log at the point of handling, not at every layer. See §1.13.
  • Use structured fields, not string interpolation. slog.Int("user_id", id) is queryable; fmt.Sprintf("user %d", id) is not.
  • slog uses any for the key/value form, so an odd number of arguments produces a !BADKEY entry rather than a compile error. LogAttrs avoids this.

#5.7 strings, strconv, regexp

String concatenation in a loop with += is O(n²) — each concatenation allocates a new string and copies everything. strings.Builder is O(n). This is one of the most impactful easy fixes in Go code.

regexp

Performance note: Go's regexp uses RE2, which guarantees linear time — it cannot suffer catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS). The tradeoff is no backreferences and no lookahead. This is the right trade for a server processing untrusted input.

Do not use regex where strings will do. strings.Contains is dramatically faster than a regex match for a literal substring.

#5.8 database/sql

sql.DB is a pool, not a connection. Create one per database for the lifetime of the process and share it — it is safe for concurrent use. Creating one per request is a serious bug.

Pool sizing: MaxOpenConns across all your replicas must stay under the database's connection limit. Ten pods × 25 connections = 250 connections; Postgres defaults to 100. This is a very common production outage.

Querying

Two mandatory lines people forget: defer rows.Close() and rows.Err(). Missing Close leaks a pooled connection until GC; missing Err() silently swallows a mid-iteration failure so you return a partial result set as if it were complete. sqlclosecheck and rowserrcheck in golangci-lint catch both.

Transactions

defer tx.Rollback() immediately after BeginTx is the standard idiom — it guarantees cleanup on any error path, and is a harmless no-op once Commit succeeds.

Prepared statements

Worth it when executing the same query many times in a loop. For one-off queries, QueryContext with arguments is already parameterized and safe — you do not need Prepare for SQL injection safety.

Avoiding N+1

N+1 is the most common cause of a slow endpoint. Look for a database call inside a loop.

Never build SQL with string concatenation:

Placeholders differ by driver: $1, $2 for Postgres, ? for MySQL and SQLite.

#Part 5 Review Checklist

Part 6

Building REST APIs: Gin

#6.1 Framework vs net/http

Use net/http alone when: the service is small, you want zero dependencies, you're building a library, or you're on Go 1.22+ where the standard mux handles method and path matching.

Use a framework when: you want request binding and validation out of the box, a middleware ecosystem, route groups, and consistent error responses without writing them yourself.

The honest comparison:

net/http (1.22+)GinFiberChiEcho
Foundationstdlibnet/httpfasthttpnet/httpnet/http
Routingmethod + wildcardsradix treeradix treeradix treeradix tree
Binding/validationmanualbuilt-inbuilt-inmanualbuilt-in
stdlib middleware compatible—with adapternoyeswith adapter
Dependenciesnonemoderatemoderate~nonemoderate

chi deserves special mention: it is http.Handler all the way down, so every piece of stdlib middleware works unmodified, and you can remove it later without rewriting handlers. If you want a router and nothing else, chi is the lowest-risk choice.

Gin is chosen here because it's the most widely deployed and the concepts transfer.

#6.2 Gin fundamentals

The Context object

*gin.Context carries the request, the response writer, path params, and a per-request key-value store. It is not context.Context — use c.Request.Context() when you need the real one to pass downstream.

Never store *gin.Context beyond the request or pass it to a goroutine that outlives the handler. Use c.Copy() if you must:

#6.3 Request binding and validation

Binding methods: ShouldBindJSON, ShouldBindQuery, ShouldBindUri, ShouldBindHeader, ShouldBind (content-type aware), ShouldBindWith.

Prefer the ShouldBind* family. The Bind* variants write a 400 and set the response themselves, which prevents you from formatting errors consistently.

Human-readable validation errors

Raw validator errors are unreadable to API consumers. Translating them is a small amount of work that meaningfully improves your API.

Custom validators

#6.4 Error handling middleware

Centralize error-to-response translation so handlers stay thin.

Never return raw internal error text on a 5xx. Database errors leak table names, query structure, and sometimes credentials.

#6.5 File uploads, streaming, pagination

Pagination

Offset pagination — simple, but OFFSET 100000 makes the database scan and discard 100,000 rows:

Cursor pagination — the correct choice for large or frequently-changing datasets:

Cursor pagination is O(1) regardless of depth and does not skip or duplicate rows when items are inserted mid-pagination. Offset pagination does both.

#6.6 Authentication

JWT — full flow

The algorithm check is not optional. The classic JWT attack sets alg: none or switches HS256 to RS256 to make the public key act as an HMAC secret. Always assert the expected method.

Auth middleware

c.Abort() (or AbortWithStatusJSON) is essential — without it, the handler still runs after the middleware returns.

Refresh tokens and revocation

JWTs are stateless, so you cannot invalidate one before it expires — unless you add state. The standard approach:

  1. Short access token (15 min), long refresh token (7 days).
  2. Store refresh tokens in Redis or the database, keyed by user, so they can be deleted on logout.
  3. Rotate on use: each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old one is reused, that indicates theft — revoke the entire family.
  4. Denylist access tokens by jti in Redis with a TTL equal to the remaining token lifetime, for immediate revocation (logout-everywhere, account compromise).

Where to store tokens client-side: httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies are safer than localStorage, which is readable by any XSS. Cookies then require CSRF protection — see §13.1.

API key auth

Store API keys hashed, exactly like passwords. A database dump should not hand over working credentials.

OAuth2

The state parameter check is mandatory. Without it, an attacker can trick a user into linking the attacker's account.

#6.7 Authorization: RBAC and ABAC

RBAC

ABAC — attribute-based, for ownership checks

Return 404, not 403, when the user shouldn't know the resource exists. A 403 confirms existence, which is an information leak on private resources.

For complex policy, casbin implements RBAC/ABAC with an external policy file, and OPA (Open Policy Agent) externalizes it entirely. Both are worth it only when policy genuinely changes independently of code.

#6.8 Rate limiting middleware

The cleanup goroutine is not optional. Without it, every unique IP that ever hits your service stays in the map — an unbounded leak that a scanner will happily exploit.

Distributed rate limiting with Redis

Running the check as a Lua script makes it atomic — a read-then-write in Go would let concurrent requests both pass the limit. More in Part 9.

#6.9 Structuring a production Gin project

The critical rule: service and repository must not import gin. If they do, you cannot test them without an HTTP request, and you cannot reuse them from a worker or CLI.

Config management

Fail fast at startup on missing config. A service that boots successfully and fails on the first request that touches the database is much worse than one that refuses to start.

viper is the heavier alternative supporting files, env, and remote config. For a 12-factor service, environment variables alone are usually right.

#6.10 OpenAPI documentation

The honest tradeoff: annotation-driven docs drift from reality, because nothing enforces that the annotation matches the code. The alternative — writing the OpenAPI spec first and generating server stubs with oapi-codegen — keeps them in sync by construction. For a public API, spec-first is the better discipline.

#6.11 Worked example: complete CRUD API

Bringing it together. cmd/server/main.go:

Handler test:

#Part 6 Review Checklist

Part 7

Fiber, gRPC, and GraphQL

#7.1 Fiber and fasthttp

What fasthttp actually costs you
