Fiber is built on fasthttp, not net/http. fasthttp achieves its performance by reusing request and response objects and avoiding allocations — which produces a specific and important set of constraints:

  1. No net/http compatibility. No stdlib middleware, no http.Handler, no httptest. The ecosystem is separate.
  2. Context values are reused after the handler returns. Any []byte or string you hold from c.Params(), c.Body(), or headers is invalid once the handler returns. You must copy: id := utils.CopyString(c.Params("id")). This is the number one Fiber bug — a value passed to a goroutine or cached silently becomes another request's data.
  3. No HTTP/2 support in fasthttp. If you need HTTP/2 or gRPC-Web on the same port, Fiber cannot do it.
  4. Smaller ecosystem for tracing, metrics, and auth integrations.

When to pick which

Gin/Chi/Echo (net/http): default choice. Ecosystem compatibility, HTTP/2, standard tooling.

Fiber: you have benchmarked and proven that HTTP parsing is your bottleneck — which for most services it is not. The bottleneck is almost always the database.

Honest assessment: the throughput difference in synthetic benchmarks rarely survives contact with a real service that spends 20ms in Postgres. Choose Fiber for its API if you like it, not for benchmark numbers you won't observe.

Migration notes

If you must move Gin → Fiber: handler signatures change (func(*gin.Context) → func(*fiber.Ctx) error), error handling becomes return-based, and every retained string needs a CopyString. Budget for the middleware being rewritten entirely.

#7.2 gRPC from scratch

Protocol Buffers

Toolchain

In practice use buf instead of raw protoc — it handles dependencies, linting, and breaking-change detection:

Server implementation

Always embed UnimplementedXServer. It means adding a method to the proto doesn't break compilation of existing servers.

Always use the generated getters (req.GetId()) rather than req.Id — the getter is nil-safe.

#7.3 The four RPC types

Unary — request/response

Shown above. The default.

Server streaming

Client:

Client streaming

Bidirectional streaming

A gRPC stream is not safe for concurrent Send from multiple goroutines. Serialize sends through a single goroutine, as above.

#7.4 Interceptors

Streaming interceptors use grpc.StreamServerInterceptor with the same shape. grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor and ChainStreamInterceptor compose them.

#7.5 gRPC error handling and gRPC-Gateway

Status codes

gRPC codeHTTP equivalentWhen
OK200success
InvalidArgument400client sent bad data
Unauthenticated401missing/invalid credentials
PermissionDenied403authenticated but not allowed
NotFound404resource doesn't exist
AlreadyExists409duplicate create
ResourceExhausted429rate limited / quota
FailedPrecondition400system state prevents the operation
Aborted409concurrency conflict, retry may work
Unavailable503transient, retry with backoff
DeadlineExceeded504timed out
Internal500bug on our side

Unavailable and Aborted are the retryable ones. FailedPrecondition explicitly is not.

Rich errors

gRPC-Gateway — REST and gRPC from one definition

You now serve gRPC on :50051 for internal services and REST/JSON on :8080 for browsers and third parties, from one schema.

#7.6 Protobuf versioning and compatibility

Safe changes (backward compatible):

  • Add a new field with a new number
  • Add a new method to a service
  • Add a new enum value (as long as clients handle unknown values)
  • Rename a field (the number is what's on the wire, not the name)

Breaking changes (never do these to a deployed schema):

  • Change a field's number — silently misinterprets data
  • Change a field's type (except among compatible integer types)
  • Reuse a deleted field's number — old clients will parse new data into the old field
  • Remove a required behaviour clients depend on

Always reserved deleted fields:

Enum rule: the zero value must be _UNSPECIFIED, because proto3 cannot distinguish an unset enum from the zero value.

buf breaking --against in CI is the enforcement mechanism. Without it, someone will eventually renumber a field and corrupt production data.

#7.7 GraphQL with gqlgen

Resolvers

Dataloaders — solving N+1

The query { products(first: 100) { reviews { author { name } } } } triggers 1 + 100 + N queries without batching.

The loader collects keys requested within a short window, issues one batched query, and distributes results. A GraphQL server without dataloaders will not survive production traffic.

GraphQL-specific production concerns

  • Query depth limiting — a nested query can be exponentially expensive. extension.FixedComplexityLimit.
  • Query cost analysis — assign a cost per field, reject queries over a budget.
  • Disable introspection in production for non-public APIs.
  • Persisted queries — clients send a hash instead of a query string; the server only executes queries from an allowlist.

When GraphQL is worth it: many diverse clients with different data needs, a mobile app minimizing round trips, a BFF aggregating multiple services. When it isn't: a single frontend consuming a single service — you get all the complexity and none of the benefit.

#Part 7 Review Checklist

Part 8

Databases and Data Access

#8.1 PostgreSQL and MySQL drivers

parseTime=true is mandatory for MySQL or DATETIME columns scan into []byte instead of time.Time.

pgx native mode (not through database/sql) is significantly faster — it uses the binary protocol, supports Postgres-specific types (arrays, JSONB, ranges) natively, and has built-in batching. Use pgxpool directly for new Postgres services.

Connection strings and TLS

sslmode=require is not secure. It encrypts but does not verify who you're talking to. Production should be verify-full.

Never hardcode connection strings. Load from environment or a secret store, and ensure they never reach logs — a %v on a config struct will happily print your database password.

#8.2 GORM in depth

CRUD and associations

Hooks

Hooks are convenient and dangerous — they run implicitly, so behaviour appears from nowhere when reading the calling code. Use them for mechanical concerns (ID generation, timestamps), never for business logic.

GORM's real downsides

Be clear-eyed about these:

  1. N+1 by default. Associations are lazily loaded unless you Preload. It's easy to write a loop that issues a query per iteration without noticing.
  2. Reflection-heavy — meaningfully slower than database/sql or sqlc. Usually irrelevant next to network latency, but real in high-throughput paths.
  3. Generated SQL is hard to predict. Complex queries produce SQL you didn't intend, and debugging means enabling the logger and reading it.
  4. The zero-value update trap shown above silently drops updates. This bites everyone once.
  5. AutoMigrate is not a migration system. It adds columns and indexes but never drops or renames, and has no version history or rollback. Do not use it in production.
  6. Soft delete leaks everywhere. Every raw query you write must remember deleted_at IS NULL, and unique indexes must account for soft-deleted rows.
  7. Error handling requires errors.Is(err, gorm.ErrRecordNotFound) — easy to forget, and a missing row otherwise looks like success with a zero-value struct.

Verdict: GORM speeds up CRUD-heavy internal tools. For a service where query performance matters and the schema is stable, sqlc is the better trade.

#8.3 sqlc — type-safe SQL generation

Generates fully typed Go:

The honest comparison

GORMsqlcQuery builder (squirrel)
You writeGoSQLGo
Type safetyruntimecompile timepartial
SQL visibilityhiddenexplicitassembled
Dynamic querieseasyhardeasy
Performancereflection overheadnear rawnear raw
Learning curveGORM's APISQL you knowbuilder API
Schema change safetyruntime failurebuild failureruntime failure

sqlc's killer feature: it validates your SQL against your actual schema at generation time. Rename a column, and sqlc generate fails — not production.

sqlc's real limitation: dynamic queries. A filter with eight optional conditions is awkward. The workarounds are the ($1::type IS NULL OR col = $1) pattern shown above, or dropping to raw SQL with a builder for that one query.

A pragmatic combination: sqlc for the 90% of queries that are static, plus squirrel or raw SQL for the handful of genuinely dynamic search endpoints.

#8.4 Migrations

Embedding migrations in the binary:

Zero-downtime migrations: expand/contract

During a rolling deploy, old and new code run simultaneously. Any migration must be compatible with both.

Renaming a column — never do it in one step. Instead:

Four deploys for one rename. That is the actual cost of zero downtime.

Other rules:

  • Adding a NOT NULL column requires a default, or it fails against existing rows. Add nullable → backfill → add the constraint.
  • CREATE INDEX locks the table in Postgres. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY — which cannot run inside a transaction, so the migration needs -- migrate:no-transaction or equivalent.
  • Batch large backfills. A single UPDATE over 10 million rows holds locks and bloats WAL. Loop in batches of a few thousand with a pause.
  • Never destroy data in a migration you can't reverse without a verified backup.

#8.5 Transactions in depth

Isolation levels

LevelPreventsAllows
Read Uncommitted—dirty reads (Postgres treats this as Read Committed)
Read Committeddirty readsnon-repeatable reads, phantoms
Repeatable Read+ non-repeatable readsphantoms (Postgres also blocks these)
Serializableeverything— (but transactions may abort)

Postgres defaults to Read Committed. MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read.

Serializable is not free. Postgres implements it optimistically — transactions run and are aborted at commit if a conflict is detected. Your code must handle 40001 serialization_failure by retrying.

Retry with backoff

Serialization failures surface at Commit(), not at the failing statement. Retry logic that only wraps the statements misses them.

Deadlock avoidance

Same principle as mutex ordering (§3.8): acquire row locks in a consistent global order.

Distributed transactions — why to avoid them

Two-phase commit across services requires every participant to hold locks until the coordinator decides. If the coordinator dies mid-protocol, participants are blocked indefinitely. It couples availability of all services to the least available one, and most modern datastores don't implement it well.

Use the Saga pattern instead (§11.6): a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions for rollback. You trade atomicity for availability and accept eventual consistency — which is almost always the right trade for a distributed system.

#8.6 MongoDB in Go

Indexes

Compound index field order follows the ESR rule: Equality, Sort, Range.

Transactions (require a replica set)

SQL vs NoSQL — the honest guidance

Choose Postgres when: you have relations, you need transactions across entities, you want a schema enforced by the database, your queries are ad-hoc and varied, or you need strong consistency. This covers most applications.

Choose MongoDB when: documents are genuinely self-contained and read as a unit, your schema varies per document, or you're storing scraped/ingested data whose shape you don't control.

A note that applies broadly: Postgres has JSONB with GIN indexing, so "I need flexible fields" is not by itself a reason to leave SQL. You can have a rigid core schema plus a flexible JSONB column, and query into it efficiently.

#8.7 Connection pool tuning

Sizing:

A common formula for a CPU-bound database is connections ≈ (2 × cores) + effective_spindle_count. In practice, start at 25 per replica, measure db.Stats().WaitCount and WaitDuration, and adjust.

More connections is not faster. Beyond the database's parallelism, extra connections add context-switching and lock contention. A pool that is too large turns a queue in your app into a queue in the database, where it's harder to observe.

ConnMaxLifetime matters more than people expect. Without it, connections pinned to a failed-over primary never rotate, and a load balancer in front of your database never rebalances. Five minutes is a reasonable default.

#8.8 Read replicas, routing, and sharding

Read/write splitting

Replication lag is the trap. A user creates a product, is redirected to the product page, and the replica hasn't caught up — they see a 404 for their own creation. Either route reads to the primary for a short window after a write (as above), or make the UI optimistic.

Sharding from the application layer

What sharding costs you: no cross-shard joins, no cross-shard transactions, no global ORDER BY without a scatter-gather, and resharding is a major project. Modulo-based sharding in particular makes adding a shard require rehashing everything — use consistent hashing or a lookup table if growth is likely.

Do not shard prematurely. A single well-indexed Postgres instance handles far more than most teams assume. Exhaust vertical scaling, read replicas, caching, and query optimization first.

#Part 8 Review Checklist

Part 9

Caching with Redis

#9.1 Redis data types

TypeUse forKey commands
Stringcached JSON, counters, flagsGET SET SETEX INCR
Hashobjects with independently-updated fieldsHGET HSET HGETALL HINCRBY
Listqueues, recent-items feedsLPUSH RPOP LRANGE BLPOP
Setunique membership, tagsSADD SISMEMBER SINTER
Sorted Setleaderboards, rate limiting, priority queues, time-ordered indexesZADD ZRANGE ZRANGEBYSCORE ZREMRANGEBYSCORE
Streamappend-only event log with consumer groupsXADD XREADGROUP XACK
HyperLogLogapproximate unique counts at tiny memory costPFADD PFCOUNT
Bitmapdense boolean flags (daily active users)SETBIT GETBIT BITCOUNT

Sorted sets are the most under-used and most powerful. Rate limiting, delayed job queues, time-series indexes, and leaderboards are all sorted sets.

#9.2 go-redis

Basic operations

redis.Nil is not an error — it means the key doesn't exist. Treating it as an error is the single most common go-redis mistake, and it turns every cache miss into a 500.

Pipelining is the biggest easy win. 100 individual SET calls are 100 round trips; a pipeline is one. On a 1ms network that's 100ms versus 1ms.

Never use KEYS * in production. It blocks the entire server while scanning every key. Use SCAN with a cursor.

#9.3 Caching patterns

Cache-aside (lazy loading) — the default

A cache failure must degrade to a slow request, never to an error. If Redis being down takes your service down, the cache has made you less reliable, not more.

Write-through and write-behind

Write-through: write to cache and database synchronously. Cache is always consistent; writes are slower.

Write-behind (write-back): write to cache, return, flush to the database asynchronously. Fast writes, but you lose data if the process dies before the flush. Appropriate for metrics and view counters; never for orders or payments.

Cache stampede prevention

When a hot key expires, every concurrent request misses and hits the database simultaneously. This is how a cache expiry becomes an outage.

Solution 1: singleflight (in-process)

Note singleflight is per-process. With 10 replicas you get 10 database calls instead of 1000 — a 100× reduction, which is usually enough.

Solution 2: distributed lock

Solution 3: probabilistic early expiration

Solution 4: jittered TTLs. If you populate 10,000 keys at once with the same TTL, they all expire at once. Add randomness:

This one line prevents a whole class of thundering-herd incident and costs nothing.

#9.4 Redis rate limiting

Covered in §6.8. The three algorithms:

Fixed window — simplest, but allows 2× the limit at a window boundary (100 requests at 0:59 and 100 at 1:01).

Sliding window log — a sorted set of timestamps, trimmed on each request. Exact, but memory grows with the limit.

Token bucket — allows bursts up to the bucket size, refills at a steady rate. Usually the best user experience.

Lua scripts run atomically in Redis. This is the only correct way to implement check-then-act logic — doing it in Go with separate GET and SET calls has a race between them.

#9.5 Pub/Sub and Streams

Pub/Sub — fire and forget

Pub/Sub has no persistence and no delivery guarantee. A subscriber that is down when a message is published never receives it. Use it for cache invalidation broadcasts and live UI updates — never for anything that must not be lost.

Streams — persistent, with consumer groups

Streams give you persistence, consumer groups, acknowledgement, and replay — a genuine lightweight message queue. Always set MaxLen, or the stream grows until Redis runs out of memory.

#9.6 Distributed locks

The ownership check in Release is essential. Without it: your process stalls, the TTL expires, another process acquires the lock, your process resumes and deletes their lock. Now two processes hold it.

Redlock and its criticism

Redlock acquires the lock on a majority of N independent Redis masters. Martin Kleppmann's well-known critique argues it does not provide the safety it claims under clock drift and process pauses (GC, VM suspension), because a lock can expire while the holder believes it still holds it. Antirez responded; the debate is worth reading.

Practical guidance:

  • For efficiency (avoid duplicate work, don't send the email twice) a Redis lock is fine. Occasional double execution is a cost, not a catastrophe.
  • For correctness (never double-charge a card) do not rely on a distributed lock. Use a database transaction with a unique constraint, or a fencing token that the protected resource validates and monotonically increases.

Always set a TTL. A lock without one becomes permanent when the holder crashes.

#9.7 Persistence and durability

RDB (snapshots): periodic point-in-time dumps. Compact, fast restarts, but you lose everything since the last snapshot.

AOF (append-only file): logs every write. appendfsync everysec is the usual setting — at most one second of data lost. Larger files, slower restart.

Both together is the common production configuration: AOF for durability, RDB for fast recovery.

What this means for your code: if Redis is a cache, persistence barely matters — a cold cache refills. If Redis is your rate limiter, a restart resets counters, briefly allowing more traffic. If Redis is a queue (Streams), persistence is essential and you should treat it with the same care as a database.

Set maxmemory and an eviction policy:

Policies: noeviction (writes fail — right for a queue), allkeys-lru (right for a pure cache), volatile-lru (only keys with a TTL). The default is noeviction, which means a cache that fills up starts returning write errors rather than evicting. Set this explicitly.

#9.8 Cache invalidation

"There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things."

Strategies

TTL only — simplest. Accept staleness up to the TTL. Correct for data where staleness is tolerable (product listings, search results).

Explicit invalidation on write:

Delete, don't update. Writing the new value into the cache introduces a race: two concurrent writers can leave the cache holding the older value. Deleting is idempotent and safe.

Versioned keys — sidestep invalidation entirely:

Old versions are never read again and expire naturally. Costs memory, eliminates a class of bug.

Tag-based invalidation:

The classic pitfalls

  1. Invalidating before the write commits — a concurrent read repopulates the cache with the old value, and the cache is now permanently stale. Always invalidate after commit.
  2. Cache/DB inconsistency on partial failure — the write succeeds, the invalidation fails. TTL is your backstop; this is why "cache forever" is dangerous.
  3. Thundering herd — covered in §9.3.
  4. Caching negative results without thought — caching "not found" prevents a database hammer from a scanner, but means a newly-created resource 404s until the TTL expires. Use a short negative TTL (seconds).
  5. Unbounded key growth — every cached key needs a TTL. A key without one lives until eviction, and with noeviction that means forever.

#Part 9 Review Checklist

Part 10

Message Queues and Async Processing

#10.1 Why async processing exists

Three reasons, in order of importance:

  1. Decoupling. The producer doesn't need the consumer to be up. An order can be accepted even when the email service is down.
  2. Backpressure. A queue absorbs a traffic spike that would otherwise overwhelm a downstream service. The queue grows instead of the service falling over.
  3. Retry semantics. A failed job can be retried automatically, with backoff, without the user's HTTP request hanging.

The cost: eventual consistency, harder debugging (the work happens elsewhere, later), operational surface (another system to run), and the requirement that every consumer be idempotent.

When to go async: anything slow (email, PDF generation, image processing, third-party APIs), anything that can fail and should be retried, anything the user doesn't need to wait for.

When not to: anything the user needs the result of immediately. Do not make a synchronous read asynchronous.

#10.2 RabbitMQ concepts

RabbitMQ implements AMQP. The mental model:

Producers never publish to queues directly. They publish to an exchange, which routes based on bindings.

Exchange types

Direct — routes to queues whose binding key exactly matches the routing key.

Topic — pattern matching with * (one word) and # (zero or more words).

Fanout — broadcasts to every bound queue, ignoring the routing key. Used for event broadcast.

Headers — routes on message headers instead of the routing key. Rarely needed.

Topic exchanges cover most real use cases. Start there.

#10.3 RabbitMQ in Go

Publisher with confirms

Without publisher confirms, Publish returning nil means "written to a socket", not "the broker has it". A broker crash loses the message silently.

DeliveryMode: amqp.Persistent plus a durable queue is required for a message to survive a broker restart. Both, not one.

Consumer with manual ack and QoS

Three critical settings:

  1. autoAck: false. With auto-ack, a message is removed the instant it's delivered — a crash mid-processing loses it.
  2. Qos(prefetch, ...). Without a prefetch limit, RabbitMQ pushes the entire queue to the first consumer, so a second consumer sits idle and a crash loses everything in flight. Start at 10 and tune.
  3. Nack(multiple: false, requeue: false). Requeuing a permanently-failing message creates an infinite loop that burns CPU forever. Send it to a dead-letter queue instead.

Reconnection

Real deployments need reconnection handling — network blips and broker restarts are normal:

The amqp091-go library does not reconnect automatically. This is the most commonly missed piece.

#10.4 Reliability patterns

Dead letter queues

A DLQ turns a silent message loss into a visible, inspectable list of failures. Alert on DLQ depth. A growing DLQ means something is broken.

Retry with exponential backoff

Delayed retry via a TTL'd holding queue:

Multiple retry queues with increasing TTLs (30s, 5m, 30m) give you exponential backoff. Track the attempt count in a header and give up into the DLQ after N:

Idempotent consumers

At-least-once delivery is the norm. Your consumer will receive duplicates — after a network blip, a redelivery, or a retry. It must handle that.

Better than deduplication: make the operation naturally idempotent.

A unique constraint in the database is a stronger guarantee than any application-level check.

#10.5 Kafka

The mental model difference

RabbitMQ is a task queue. Messages are consumed and removed. Routing is rich. Good for "do this work."

Kafka is a distributed commit log. Messages are appended and retained for a configured period regardless of consumption. Multiple independent consumer groups read the same data at their own offsets. Good for "this happened."

Ordering is per-partition, not per-topic. Messages with the same key go to the same partition, so keying by order_id guarantees ordering for that order. There is no global ordering.

Parallelism is bounded by partition count. Ten consumers on a three-partition topic leaves seven idle.

kafka-go

FetchMessage + CommitMessages gives at-least-once. ReadMessage auto-commits before you've processed, which is at-most-once and loses messages on a crash.

RequiredAcks: RequireAll is what makes a write durable. RequireOne acknowledges from the leader only and loses data if the leader fails before replication.

Choosing between them

RabbitMQKafka
Modeltask queueevent log
After consumptiondeletedretained
Replaynoyes
Multiple independent consumersseparate queuesconsumer groups on one topic
Routingrich (topic/direct/fanout)topic + partition key only
Orderingper-queueper-partition
Throughputhighvery high
Operational complexitymoderatehigh
Per-message TTL/priorityyesno

Choose RabbitMQ for: background jobs, task distribution, complex routing, per-message priorities. Choose Kafka for: event streaming, multiple teams consuming the same events, audit logs, replay requirements, very high throughput.

For most application backends, RabbitMQ or a Redis-backed queue is sufficient and much simpler to run.

#10.6 Task queues in Go: Asynq

Asynq is the closest Go equivalent to Celery — Redis-backed, with scheduling, retries, priorities, and a web UI.

Task definition

asynq.SkipRetry is important — retrying a permanently-invalid payload five times with backoff wastes a worker slot for minutes.

Enqueueing

asynq.Unique and asynq.TaskID are how you make enqueueing itself idempotent — critical when the enqueue happens inside a retried HTTP handler.

Worker server with priority queues

Asynq handles graceful shutdown on SIGTERM — in-flight tasks complete before exit.

Monitoring UI:

Machinery — the alternative

Machinery supports multiple brokers (Redis, RabbitMQ, AMQP, SQS) and adds chains, groups, and chords (workflow primitives Celery users will recognize). It's more flexible and correspondingly more complex.

Choose Asynq for Redis-only, simplicity, and the excellent monitoring. Choose Machinery if you need a non-Redis broker or workflow composition.

Building a minimal task queue

Understanding what these libraries do:

BRPOPLPUSH (or BLMOVE in newer Redis) is the key primitive — it makes dequeue crash-safe. This is roughly what Asynq does, plus retries, priorities, and observability.

#10.7 Scheduled jobs and distributed cron

The distributed cron problem

With three replicas, robfig/cron runs your job three times. This is the single most common bug when scaling a Go service that has scheduled work.

Solution 1: leader election via a distributed lock

The TTL must be shorter than the interval but long enough that a slow instance doesn't let a second one start.

Solution 2: Asynq's scheduler (recommended)

The scheduler enqueues one task; exactly one worker picks it up. Running multiple scheduler replicas is safe — Asynq deduplicates. This is the cleanest solution because it reuses the queue's existing guarantees.

Solution 3: Kubernetes CronJob — a separate pod per execution. Clean isolation, but startup latency and a separate deployment artifact.

#10.8 The outbox pattern

The dual-write problem: you need to commit a database change and publish an event. There is no transaction spanning both.

If the publish fails or the process dies between the two, the order exists but no downstream system knows.

The outbox pattern: write the event to the database in the same transaction.

The relay

This gives at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once — a crash after publishing but before the UPDATE republishes the event. Consumers must be idempotent (§10.4). That is the standard, achievable guarantee in distributed systems.

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is what makes the relay horizontally scalable: multiple instances grab disjoint batches without blocking each other.

Alternative: Change Data Capture. Debezium reads the Postgres WAL and publishes outbox inserts to Kafka automatically, removing the polling relay entirely. More infrastructure, less application code.

#Part 10 Review Checklist

Part 11

Microservices and System Design

#11.1 Monolith vs microservices

Start with a monolith. This is not conservatism; it is the empirically better default.

What microservices actually cost:

  1. Every function call becomes a network call that can fail, time out, or be slow.
  2. No distributed transactions. Consistency becomes your problem (§11.6).
  3. Debugging spans services. You need distributed tracing before you need it.
  4. Operational multiplication. N services means N deployments, N dashboards, N on-call runbooks.
  5. Local development gets hard. Running the system on a laptop requires docker-compose orchestration or heavy mocking.
  6. Data duplication. Each service owns its data, so the same user record exists in several shapes.

What they buy:

  1. Independent deployment — teams ship without coordinating.
  2. Independent scaling — scale the image processor without scaling the API.
  3. Fault isolation — one service failing doesn't take everything down (if you built circuit breakers).
  4. Technology heterogeneity — use Python for ML and Go for the API.
  5. Team autonomy at organizational scale.

The honest heuristic: microservices solve an organizational problem, not a technical one. With fewer than about 20 engineers, the coordination cost they save is smaller than the operational cost they add.

The modular monolith is the right middle ground: one deployable, but strict internal module boundaries with no cross-module database access. When a module genuinely needs to scale or ship independently, extracting it is straightforward because the boundary already exists.

The rule that makes extraction possible later: a module never touches another module's tables.

#11.2 Service communication

Synchronous: REST or gRPC

Use when the caller needs the answer to proceed. Costs: temporal coupling (both must be up), latency accumulation, and cascading failure risk.

Asynchronous: events

Use when the caller doesn't need a result. Gains: temporal decoupling, natural backpressure, easy fan-out. Costs: eventual consistency, harder debugging.

The choice

Latency accumulates in synchronous chains. Service A → B → C → D, each at 50ms p99, gives you 200ms minimum and much worse tail latency, because p99 compounds. Every synchronous hop is a reliability and latency multiplier.

Prefer choreography over orchestration for events. Instead of a central coordinator calling each service, each service reacts to events and emits its own. Less coupling, though harder to see the whole flow — which is why tracing matters.

#11.3 Service discovery, gateways, and BFF

Service discovery

In Kubernetes you mostly don't need it — DNS handles it. http://catalog-service.default.svc.cluster.local:8080 resolves to a Service that load-balances across pods. This covers the majority of deployments.

Outside Kubernetes, Consul is the common answer:

API gateway

A single entry point handling cross-cutting concerns so each service doesn't reimplement them: TLS termination, authentication, rate limiting, request routing, and response aggregation.

Options: Kong, Traefik, Envoy, AWS API Gateway, or a Go service you write yourself.

Keep business logic out of the gateway. A gateway that knows about orders becomes a distributed monolith with a deployment bottleneck.

Backend-for-Frontend

One backend per client type, each shaped to that client's needs:

The mobile BFF returns a compact aggregated payload to minimize round trips on a slow connection; the web BFF returns richer data. Without BFFs, every downstream service accumulates client-specific fields and endpoints.

#11.4 Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry

Setup

Instrumenting

Propagation across a queue

HTTP and gRPC propagation is automatic. Queues are not — you must carry the context yourself:

Without this, your trace stops at the queue boundary and you lose visibility into exactly the asynchronous part that's hardest to debug.

Link traces to logs by putting the trace ID in every log line:

Now a slow trace in Jaeger links directly to the log lines for that request. This combination is what makes distributed debugging tractable.

#11.5 Circuit breakers and retries

The problem

Service B is slow. Service A's requests pile up waiting. A's goroutines and connections exhaust. A becomes unavailable. A's callers pile up. The failure cascades upward.

A circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency, failing fast instead.

Have a fallback. A circuit breaker without one just fails faster. Serve stale cache, a default, or a partial response.

Retries — and how they cause outages

Rules that prevent retries from making things worse:

  1. Only retry idempotent operations. Retrying a POST that creates an order creates two orders. Use an idempotency key if you must.
  2. Only retry transient errors. 5xx, timeouts, connection refused. Never 4xx.
  3. Always jitter. Without it, N clients that failed together retry together, creating a synchronized thundering herd that keeps the recovering service down.
  4. Cap total attempts and honour the context deadline. Retries must fit inside the caller's budget.
  5. Never retry at every layer. Three layers each retrying three times is 27 requests. Retry at one layer — usually the outermost client.

Retry storms are a genuine outage cause. A service recovers, gets hit by every client's accumulated retries simultaneously, and falls over again. Circuit breakers plus jitter are the defence.

#11.6 The Saga pattern

Since distributed transactions are impractical (§8.5), sagas achieve consistency through a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions.

Orchestration — a central coordinator

Choreography — no coordinator

Orchestration: the flow is visible in one place, easy to reason about, but the coordinator is a coupling point and can become a bottleneck.

Choreography: loosely coupled and independently scalable, but no single place shows the flow. Distributed tracing becomes essential, not optional.

Rules for either:

  • Every step must be idempotent — retries and redeliveries are guaranteed.
  • Compensations must be idempotent too, and must handle "already compensated."
  • Some things cannot be compensated. You cannot un-send an email. Order steps so irreversible actions come last.
  • Persist saga state. A coordinator crash mid-saga must be recoverable.
  • Monitor stuck sagas. A saga that started and never finished is invisible without explicit alerting.

#11.7 Event sourcing and CQRS

Event sourcing

Store the sequence of events, not the current state. Current state is derived by replaying them.

What you gain: a complete audit trail, the ability to reconstruct state at any past moment, temporal queries, and debugging by replay.

What you pay: significant complexity, schema evolution of events is hard (old events must remain readable forever), rebuilding from thousands of events is slow without snapshots, and querying current state requires projections.

Snapshots mitigate the replay cost: persist state every N events and replay only from there.

CQRS

Separate the write model from the read model.

When CQRS is worth it: reads and writes have very different scaling profiles, reads need a shape that's expensive to compute from the normalized model, or you need multiple read representations (SQL for the app, Elasticsearch for search).

When it isn't: most CRUD applications. You are adding eventual consistency, a projection pipeline to maintain and monitor, and a class of bug where the read model drifts from the write model.

Be honest about eventual consistency. After a write, the read model may not reflect it for some milliseconds or seconds. The UI must handle "I just saved this and it's not showing" — usually by rendering optimistically from the command response.

#11.8 API versioning

URL path versioning — most common, most visible:

Header versioning — cleaner URLs, less discoverable:

Query parameter — easy but easy to forget:

Recommendation: URL path versioning for public APIs. It is unambiguous, cacheable, greppable in logs, and obvious in documentation.

Versioning strategy

Version at the transport layer only. Duplicating business logic per version is how you end up maintaining two systems.

Rules:

  • Additive changes don't need a version. Adding an optional field is backward compatible.
  • Removing or renaming a field does.
  • Announce deprecation with a header and a timeline:
  • Instrument version usage. You cannot retire v1 until you know nobody uses it.
  • Support at most two versions. Three is a maintenance trap.

#Part 11 Review Checklist

Part 12

Observability and Production Readiness

#12.1 Structured logging in production

Covered mechanically in §5.6. The production concerns:

Correlation IDs

Propagate the ID to every downstream call — HTTP headers, gRPC metadata, queue message headers. One ID should let you find every log line across every service for a single user action.

What to log at each level

LevelUse forExample
Debugdevelopment detail, off in productionquery parameters, cache hit/miss
Infonotable business eventsuser registered, order placed, service started
Warnrecoverable problemscache unavailable, retry succeeded, deprecated endpoint used
Errorfailures needing attentiondatabase unreachable, handler panic

Do not log at Info for every request if you have request metrics — you're paying for storage of data you have in a cheaper form. Log the exceptions.

Sampling high-volume logs

Never log

Passwords, tokens, API keys, session IDs, full card numbers, national ID numbers, or full request bodies containing personal data. A log aggregator is a lower-security environment than your database — more people have access to it, and retention is often longer.

Implementing slog.LogValuer on config and user types is the reliable way to prevent accidental secret logging.

#12.2 Metrics with Prometheus

The four metric types

Use histograms, not summaries. Summary quantiles are computed per-instance and cannot be averaged across replicas — a "p99" aggregated from summaries is mathematically meaningless. Histograms aggregate correctly.

Middleware

Cardinality is the thing that kills Prometheus. Never use an unbounded value as a label — user ID, request ID, full URL path, email. Each unique label combination is a separate time series. A user_id label with a million users is a million series and an out-of-memory Prometheus.

Exposing and using the runtime collector

That gives you go_goroutines, go_memstats_*, and go_gc_duration_seconds for free — the goroutine count is your leak detector.

RED and USE

RED — for request-driven services:

  • Rate — requests per second
  • Errors — failed requests per second
  • Duration — latency distribution

USE — for resources (CPU, memory, connection pools, queues):

  • Utilization — percent busy
  • Saturation — queued work
  • Errors — error count

Alert on symptoms, not causes. Alert on "error rate above 1%" and "p99 above 2 seconds", not on "CPU above 80%" — high CPU with healthy latency is not a problem, and low CPU with terrible latency is.

#12.3 Health checks and graceful shutdown

Liveness vs readiness — the distinction matters

Liveness: "is this process alive?" Failing it means Kubernetes restarts the pod. Readiness: "can this process serve traffic?" Failing it means Kubernetes removes it from the Service, but doesn't restart it.

Checking the database in the liveness probe is a classic outage amplifier. The database has a blip, every pod fails liveness, Kubernetes restarts all of them simultaneously, and now the recovering database is hit by a full cold-start reconnection storm. Liveness answers "is the process wedged?" — nothing more.

Graceful shutdown, done properly

Step 1 is the one everyone misses. Kubernetes removes a pod from endpoints asynchronously, and kube-proxy on each node updates its rules on its own schedule. If you shut down immediately on SIGTERM, requests are still arriving for several seconds and they get connection-refused. Failing readiness and pausing first is what makes deploys actually zero-downtime.

terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed your total shutdown time, or Kubernetes SIGKILLs you mid-drain.

#12.4 Configuration and secrets

12-factor config

Validate at startup and refuse to boot on invalid config. A service that starts with a weak secret and serves traffic is worse than one that crashes loudly in CI.

Secrets

Never in: source code, Docker images, environment variables baked into a manifest, logs, error messages.

Acceptable: injected environment variables from a secret manager, mounted files, or fetched at startup.

Kubernetes Secrets are base64, not encrypted, by default. Enable encryption at rest, or use External Secrets Operator with a real secret store.

Plan for rotation. Secrets that can never be rotated without downtime will not be rotated.

#12.5 Panic recovery

One panicking request must never take down the process.

Every goroutine you spawn needs its own recovery — a panic in a background goroutine crashes the process regardless of handler middleware (§1.13).

Use this wrapper everywhere instead of a bare go. Alert on panics_total — every panic is a bug.

#Part 12 Review Checklist

Part 13

Security

#13.1 Input validation, injection, XSS, CSRF

SQL injection

Identifiers cannot be parameterized. A dynamic ORDER BY column must be validated against an allowlist:

NoSQL injection

XSS

For a JSON API, XSS is mostly the frontend's problem — but two things matter on your side:

CSRF

CSRF only applies when the browser attaches credentials automatically — i.e. cookie-based auth. A pure Bearer-token API is not vulnerable, because the attacker's site cannot read or set your Authorization header.

SameSite=Strict blocks the cookie on cross-site requests entirely. For flows needing cross-site navigation, SameSite=Lax plus a CSRF token (gorilla/csrf) is the standard combination.

Security headers

CORS — get this right

AllowOrigins: ["*"] with AllowCredentials: true is invalid per spec and browsers reject it — but some libraries reflect the request Origin instead, which is effectively "allow everyone" and defeats the entire same-origin policy. Never reflect an arbitrary Origin.

#13.2 Password hashing and token generation

Never use MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, or any fast hash for passwords. They are designed to be fast, which is exactly wrong — a GPU computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second.

Secure random and constant-time comparison

math/rand is predictable. Seeding it with the time does not help — an attacker who sees one output can predict the rest. Every token, session ID, salt, API key, and CSRF token must come from crypto/rand.

Use subtle.ConstantTimeCompare for secrets. == on strings short-circuits at the first differing byte, leaking information about how many bytes matched through response timing.

Timing-safe user lookup

Return the same error for "no such user" and "wrong password." Distinguishing them is user enumeration.

#13.3 TLS in Go

Automatic certificates

Mutual TLS for service-to-service

Never set InsecureSkipVerify: true outside a test. It disables certificate verification entirely, making TLS provide encryption with no authentication — fully vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle. gosec flags it; do not suppress the finding.

A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) provides mTLS transparently without application changes, which is usually the better path at scale.

#13.4 Secrets handling and dependency scanning

Never log secrets

Now fmt.Printf("%v", cfg), json.Marshal(cfg), and slog.Info("config", "cfg", cfg) are all safe. Getting the value requires an explicit .Reveal() call that stands out in review.

Rotation

Support two valid secrets during a rotation window so it can happen without downtime:

Scanning

In CI:

govulncheck is better than a generic SCA tool because it analyzes whether your code actually reaches the vulnerable function — far fewer false positives, so the findings get acted on.

#13.5 OWASP API Top 10 in Go

RiskGo-specific mitigation
1. Broken Object Level AuthorizationCheck ownership in the service layer after loading the object. Middleware cannot do this. Return 404, not 403.
2. Broken AuthenticationVerify the JWT alg. Short access tokens. Argon2/bcrypt. Rate-limit login. Identical error for bad user and bad password.
3. Broken Object Property Level AuthUse explicit request DTOs, never bind directly into your domain model — otherwise a client can set is_admin: true. Use DisallowUnknownFields.
4. Unrestricted Resource Consumptionhttp.MaxBytesReader, pagination limits (max=100), query timeouts, rate limiting, GraphQL depth limits.
5. Broken Function Level AuthorizationDeny by default. Apply auth middleware at the group level, then opt specific routes into public.
6. Unrestricted Access to Business FlowsRate limit by business action, not just by endpoint. CAPTCHA on signup. Detect automation.
7. Server Side Request ForgeryValidate and allowlist outbound URLs. Block private IP ranges and link-local (169.254.169.254 is the cloud metadata endpoint).
8. Security Misconfigurationgin.ReleaseMode in production. Disable pprof/debug endpoints publicly. Security headers. Correct CORS.
9. Improper Inventory ManagementVersion your API. Retire old versions. Document every endpoint. Instrument usage.
10. Unsafe Consumption of APIsValidate third-party responses like user input. Timeouts on every outbound call. Circuit breakers.

#3 in detail — mass assignment

Never bind a request body directly into your database model. Always go through a DTO listing exactly the mutable fields.

#7 in detail — SSRF

The cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) is the highest-value SSRF target — it returns IAM credentials. ip.IsLinkLocalUnicast() blocks it. Note this check is still vulnerable to DNS rebinding; the robust fix is a custom DialContext that validates the IP at connection time.

#Part 13 Review Checklist

Part 14

Deployment and Infrastructure

#14.1 Dockerizing a Go service

What each piece does:

  • Copying go.mod/go.sum before the source means the dependency layer only invalidates when dependencies change — the single biggest build-cache win.
  • --mount=type=cache persists the module and build cache across builds (BuildKit).
  • CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a fully static binary, which is what allows a distroless or scratch base.
  • -s -w strips symbols and DWARF, cutting binary size substantially.
  • -trimpath removes local filesystem paths from the binary — reproducibility and a minor information leak avoided.
  • distroless nonroot has no shell, no package manager, and runs as a non-root user. Dramatically smaller attack surface than Alpine.

Base image comparison:

alpine~7 MByesmusl libc; useful when you need to exec in
debian:slim~80 MByesonly if you need cgo or system libraries

If you use scratch, copy the certificates yourself or every outbound HTTPS call fails with an opaque x509 error:

#14.2 Docker Compose for local development

condition: service_healthy is the important detail. Without it, depends_on only waits for the container to start, not for Postgres to accept connections — so your app crashes on boot in a race that appears intermittently.

Hot reload with air:

#14.3 Kubernetes for a Go backend

The Go-specific settings that matter most:

  • GOMEMLIMIT at ~90% of the memory limit. Without it, the Go heap grows past the container limit and the kernel OOM-kills you with no Go-level error, no stack trace, and nothing in your logs. This is the most common mystery crash in containerized Go.
  • GOMAXPROCS matching the CPU limit, or use automaxprocs (§2.3). Otherwise Go creates one P per host core and thrashes under CFS throttling.
  • terminationGracePeriodSeconds > shutdown timeout, or Kubernetes SIGKILLs you mid-drain.
  • maxUnavailable: 0 keeps capacity constant during a rollout.
  • A PodDisruptionBudget stops a node drain from taking every replica at once.

Migrations as an init container

Caveat: with three replicas, three init containers race to migrate. golang-migrate takes an advisory lock so this is safe, but a Kubernetes Job run before the rollout is cleaner and gives you a clear failure point.

#14.4 CI/CD with GitHub Actions

Deploy by immutable SHA tag, never latest. latest makes rollback ambiguous and means you cannot tell which code is running.

#14.5 Zero-downtime deployment

Rolling update — the default

New pods start, pass readiness, receive traffic, then old pods drain. This only works if your application cooperates:

  1. Graceful shutdown with a readiness pause (§12.3).
  2. Backward-compatible database migrations (§8.4) — old and new code run simultaneously.
  3. Backward-compatible API changes — the old frontend may still be running.

Blue/green

Two full environments; switch traffic at the load balancer atomically.

Pros: instant rollback, and you test the real environment before exposing it. Cons: double the infrastructure cost, and database schema must serve both.

Canary

Route a small percentage to the new version and watch metrics.

With a service mesh you get real percentage control and automatic rollback on metric regression:

Canary is the safest strategy for a high-traffic service, because a bad deploy affects 5% of users for two minutes rather than 100% until someone notices.

Feature flags — decoupling deploy from release

Deploy the code dark, enable it for 1% of users, watch, ramp up. Turning a feature off is a config change, not a rollback — seconds instead of minutes, and no risk of reverting unrelated changes shipped in the same deploy.

#15.1 The system

Rivyou Catalog Service — a product catalog and review platform touching every layer in this document.

Requirements

  • REST API for web and mobile clients
  • gRPC API for internal service-to-service calls
  • Postgres for products, reviews, and users
  • Redis for caching and rate limiting
  • Asynq for asynchronous work (review moderation, search indexing, email)
  • JWT authentication with refresh rotation
  • Full observability: structured logs, Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces
  • Deployed to Kubernetes with zero-downtime rollouts

Architecture

    LB --> API[Catalog API<br/>Gin + gRPC]

    API -->|read/write| PG[(PostgreSQL<br/>primary)]

Technology choices and reasoning

ChoiceWhyAlternative rejected because
GinMature, large ecosystem, net/http compatibleFiber: fasthttp breaks stdlib middleware and HTTP/2, and HTTP parsing is not our bottleneck
sqlcCompile-time SQL validation against the real schemaGORM: N+1 by default, unpredictable SQL, and AutoMigrate isn't a migration system
golang-migrateVersioned, reversible, embeddableAutoMigrate: no rollback, no history
AsynqRedis-backed (already in the stack), good monitoring, scheduler solves distributed cronRabbitMQ: another system to operate for work Redis handles; Kafka: we need a task queue, not an event log
RedisCache + rate limiter + queue backend in one systemMemcached: no data structures, no persistence, no queue
PostgreSQLRelational data, transactions, JSONB where flexibility is neededMongoDB: our data is relational; JSONB covers the flexible fields
gRPC internallyTyped contracts, streaming, generated clientsREST internally: no schema enforcement, more hand-written client code
OpenTelemetryVendor-neutral, one instrumentation for traces and metricsVendor SDK: lock-in

Project layout

Layer-by-layer summary

domain — types and sentinel errors. Imports nothing. This is what makes every other layer testable.

repository — wraps sqlc-generated queries, translates sql.ErrNoRows into domain.ErrNotFound, and adds context to errors with %w.

service — business rules, transaction boundaries, cache-aside logic, enqueueing async work, ownership checks. Takes repository interfaces, so tests use fakes. Imports no HTTP or gRPC package.

handler/http — binds and validates DTOs, calls the service, maps domain errors to status codes via c.Error() and the error middleware. Thin by design.

handler/grpc — same service calls, protobuf messages, status.Error codes.

tasks — Asynq handlers. Each one idempotent, each with SkipRetry on permanent failures.

The request path, end to end

Every step carries the same context.Context, so a client disconnect at step 1 cancels the database query at step 10.

Testing strategy

LayerApproach
domainpure unit tests, table-driven
servicefakes for repository and cache interfaces
repositoryintegration tests against a real Postgres via testcontainers, guarded by //go:build integration
handlerhttptest with a fake service
tasksdirect handler invocation with a constructed payload
end-to-enddocker-compose, a real request through the whole stack

Everything runs under -race in CI.
